en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Youth Ajaṭa, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, together with a great [assembly].
The assembly of bhikṣus numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty, along with an incalculable number of great bodhisattvas.
At that time, within the city, the first wife of General Siṃha was pregnant with a virtuous son. Then, from the heavens and the void of space, a great voice proclaimed to him, saying: "O youth!

You should embrace the Way and its teachings and contemplate the scriptures; be careful not to propagate worldly talk. Master the skillful means of the Dharma that transcends the world, speak little and use few words, and abandon secular affairs. You should return to the true meaning and not adopt flowery language or elaborate rhetoric.

When the youth heard such a voice from afar, he neither wept nor made a sound; from the very beginning, he did not manifest the appearance of an infant. For seven days his countenance remained joyful and pleasant, without any sign of distress, so that the multitude who came to behold him never grew weary of the sight.
Someone said, "This child makes no sound; what is the use of nourishing him?
His parents replied:
"This is not a matter of following past karma;
I shall raise him myself. Why is this?
Now, observing this child, his majestic bearing and countenance are upright, exquisite, and sublime beyond measure; he is not one whom ordinary people can equal—this is truly not false."
At that time, because his parents, relatives, and acquaintances saw that their son made no sound, they collectively named him "The Silent One" (Avācaka).
Thereupon, as the youth Avācaka gradually grew up until he reached the age of eight, the crowds of people from all quarters who came to observe him never grew weary.

Whenever there were those who held specific views or engaged in Dharma assemblies to analyze the meaning of the teachings, he would immediately go to them to inquire about and receive their words on the Dharma; yet, remaining silent and reflecting in stillness, he himself would say nothing.

Then, on another day, that youth, together with his parents, five kinds of relatives, friends, and acquaintances, went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to visit the Buddha. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood before the World-Honored One with palms joined. There he beheld hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of bodhisattvas from countless worlds in the ten directions, each seated upon a pure and adorned throne; seeing this, his heart was filled with great joy and a virtuous intention arose within him.
Then Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Heaven among Heavens!

This son of General Siṃha is one who is beyond speech; he is so upright, beautiful, and of such immeasurable, towering majesty that he is detached from discourse and has nothing to say. What remaining karmic retribution did this man have in his previous lives, that he was born without sound and is unable to speak?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Cease, cease!
Do not hastily treat the youth Maunī with contempt."

Why is this so? This person is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has planted many roots of merit under past buddhas, made offerings to countless Buddhas and Perfectly Awakened Ones, and having prostrated at their feet, attained the stage of non-retrogression; he shall surely realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At the time of his birth, a deity proclaimed a great sound from the void:
"O youth, you should embrace the aspiration for the Way; contemplate the scriptures and do not engage in worldly talk."

For this reason, this bodhisattva now remains silent and speaks not; for eight years he has received the teaching of compliant discipline, with single-minded focus and tongue-tied, saying nothing, practicing the four dhyānas in serene stillness.
The World-Honored One again addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“There are sentient beings who, if they can behold the Bodhisattva Wordless, will all accord with the Way of the Teaching through this wordlessness. For this reason, there is now a great assembly; I shall preach the Dharma to instruct, transform, guide, and benefit an immeasurable and incalculable multitude of people.”

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Aśabdha, just as he had envisioned, entered into samādhi and manifested a miraculous response. He caused each member of the entire assembly—the śrāvakas, the multitude of bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—to have a lotus flower, as large as a chariot wheel, miraculously born within their right palms. These flowers were of various exquisite and brilliant colors, with an immeasurable fragrance that brought joy to the hearts of all who beheld them.
Upon those lotuses were spontaneously manifested transformed bodhisattvas, sitting cross-legged with their bodies adorned by the thirty-two marks.

When the Bodhisattva Wordless beheld this great supernormal power, he prostrated himself before the World-Honored One and took refuge in him; the bodhisattvas seated upon the various lotuses likewise joined their palms, bowed low, and also took the triple refuge three times.

As soon as the Bodhisattva Wordless had uttered these words with his mouth, he prostrated himself in homage; immediately and spontaneously, the Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shook in six ways, a great sound was heard everywhere, and the gods in the sky praised him like the roll of thunder while raining down various flowers; lutes and musical instruments sounded of their own accord without being struck.

The Bodhisattva Wordless, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and brought about by his great vows, leaped into the air to a height of four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground; the assembly of great bodhisattvas did likewise.
The Silent Great Being, together with the Bodhisattvas, spoke with one voice in verse to praise the Buddha:
“Formless yet manifesting form, Nor dwelling within the realm of matter,
Desiring to transform and enlighten the multitudes, He manifests his body and imparts the teaching.”
The Buddha is a gathering beyond form, nor does he cling to the conditioned;
having transcended all numerical categories, the Guide nevertheless manifests his body.
He displays the thirty-two primary marks and the eighty secondary signs of excellence.
Adorning his body, he preaches the Dharma for the multitude.
The Dharma is without marks and likewise without sound;
it is voiceless and ungraspable, thought-free, tranquil, and subtle.
The Buddha-dharma awakens to all phenomena; dwelling beneath the Bodhi tree, that Way is without verbal instruction, for words have nothing to express.
That Dharma is formless; though one seeks its marks, they cannot be found.
Since the Dharma is signless, how could there be anything to be said?
Out of compassion for all living beings, this is the Great Benevolence of the Buddha;
though nothing is attained through discrimination, what he teaches never misses its proper time.
Thoroughly understanding that there is nothing to be attained, And comprehending emptiness so that nothing is acquired—
One who can nurture [the mind] in this way Is the meaning of "Buddha," which is beyond names.
The verbal teachings of conditioned phenomena Are spoken by the Buddhas as skillful means.
That number does not exist; it is unconditioned and lacks intrinsic nature.
Just as there is no permanent form or color, the Guide perceives the elephant through conditions;
since this dharma does not exist, he preaches this sutra for the sake of the multitude.
Furthermore, from birth until the age of eight, his mouth never uttered a word;
yet at the time of my initial birth, the various devas proclaimed with a great voice.
Because he had entered into contemplation of the scriptures, his ears did not hear those sounds.
Thus harboring the path and its practice, his mouth likewise uttered nothing.
Though speechless, he provisionally employed instruction;
though his words conveyed no [discursive] expression, by means of speech he was said to have spoken, radiating pure and wondrous light.
Recalling the vow for the Buddha-way, with the will set upon the Mahāyāna, one shall proclaim the Honored One’s teaching and attain Buddhahood, the supreme among men.
The mind of the Way cannot be grasped; it is a recollection that is wordless and signless.
Therefore it is said: "The Way is empty; by unraveling the knots, radiance is formed.
Thereupon, the youth addressed the assembled multitude:
"The Way and its verbal teachings are equal and without distinction; they cannot be seen!"

It cannot be grasped! That which can be spoken of cannot be seen; one speaks of the Way with the mind, yet people calculate the Way and seek something therein. What they dwell upon and aspire to is non-existent; where nothing can be obtained, there is no place to abide. To abide in this manner is the establishment of the Way!
The various perfections (pāramitās) are likewise thus.
As for the source of all other innumerable virtues, though they are expounded through verbal teachings, there is nothing actually spoken; it is merely sound, devoid of words.

Furthermore, it is said that regarding the practitioner of giving: one gives what should be given to those who are worthy of receiving; there is a direction toward which the gift is bestowed, abiding in the Way with equanimity toward all. One speaks of compassionate giving with the mouth, yet the teaching of the Way also practices loving-kindness. That Way is spontaneous and impartial as space. What the mind understands and articulates is reckoned by them all to be pure; that Way is universally empty and upright in this manner.

Whatever one does through bodily action, whatever one speaks through verbal expression, and whatever one conceives in the mind—all such afflictions are relinquished and given away; this is what is called the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā).
That which is encouraged and assisted is likewise so.
Generosity is not a gift bestowed by the Way; those who conceive of the Way do not rely upon generosity. These two matters are merely provisional names;
they are eternally without attachment and without form or image.
If one who thus receives the teachings of the Way practices the conduct of a bodhisattva, this is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).
For such a person, the act of giving becomes pure, because they bestow gifts without thinking of a reward.
When the ear hears the prohibitions and precepts, it does not dwell upon forms; thus there is neither arising nor ceasing. It is the same for one who observes the precepts.

If the actions of body, speech, and mind leave nothing created, then all things are non-existent; yet one still engages in discrimination, which is merely the expounding of what is formed through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
That which is spoken by the mouth is called "precept" (*śīla*) because it is based on names.
As with what is spoken by the mouth, so too is the precept itself.

These two things are both without form or image; all the karmic activities of the prohibitory precepts are merely provisional verbal expressions without fixed phrases. For one who calculates the Way, there is nothing that can be spoken.

Whatever flows from his mouth and mind, he employs these actions as prohibitive precepts to encourage and assist the Way. He speaks of the precepts as the Way and desires to illuminate them through the precepts. All things are without form, just like empty space; to be able to understand this is called the solitary practice of the retributive observance of the prohibitive precepts.
The sphere in which his aspirations roam is transcendent and peerless; he has entered the awakening of equality—a path of tireless, profound, and wondrous subtlety that is difficult to fathom.
Thereupon, he praised him, saying:
“As the Way is, so too is the speaker: Without support, it cannot be seen.”
That which is taught is without anything perceived; that which I proclaim is the Buddha-way.
One makes a vow to seek the Way, yet that which is wished for has no abiding place.
Being without abiding and without location, such is the establishment of the Way.
The various perfections (pāramitās) are thus, as are all the manifold virtues performed;
though expressed through words and entrusted to sounds, that which is spoken is without anything spoken.
That which is called "giving" (dāna), and that which is given, and that to which it should be given—[all these are likewise empty].
Those who are currently being instructed all abide in the path of equality.
What they proclaim through their speech is the practice of giving;
they expound upon the matters of the Path, and that Path is likewise spontaneous, equal to empty space.
If one can thoroughly understand the mind and that which is spoken by the mouth, all of these will be pure;
through purity of hearing, one reaches the Way.
When body, speech, and mental intention abandon all defilements, [one attains liberation].
The exhortation is likewise thus: this is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Giving does not return to the Way, nor does the Way rely upon giving;
these two are merely provisional names, without attachment and without form.
If there is no reliance or dependence, and one’s reception of the Way is like this—
if one does not harbor expectations for a reward— this is called giving. Furthermore,
if one hears of the prohibitions and precepts merely as a pretext, and does not dwell upon forms or appearances, [this is also called giving].
Neither arising nor ceasing—this is the characteristic of precepts.
The non-practice of precepts is likewise; body, speech, and mind are without distinction.
There is no action and nothing that exists; it is merely a conventional designation!
The arising of words is due to the conjunction of causes and conditions; they are merely called "prohibitory precepts.
Just as my precepts are perfectly equal, these two matters are without outflows (*anāsrava*).
All matters concerning prohibitory precepts are entirely dependent upon conventional speech.
That which is attained through the Way and its meaning is without speech and without karma.
What is spoken by the mouth and performed by the mind— the prohibitions, the precepts, and the encouragement of the Path—
when one calculates these precepts and the teachings of the Path, they are all like empty space.
"If one understands this, one walks alone yet universally enters the precepts;
thus dwelling and roaming within the Way, one abides in profound and wondrous verses that are difficult to comprehend.
The youth further addressed those gathered in the assembly:
"What is called the teaching of patience is also merely words; understanding the meaning of emptiness within emptiness is true patience.

Patience is like equality, and the three realms are likewise like it. To say that the form and category of patience are without image and without visibility, and to maintain an equanimous mind toward this—this is what is named patience."

If one can maintain emptiness and stillness as the root of patience, then sounds, scents, and flavors are merely compounded through causes and conditions; they possess no inherent existence and are but mere words. For this reason, it is proclaimed that one practices patience!
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, has taught that there are three kinds of patience: those of body, speech, and mind.
If one can thoroughly understand these forms of patience, this is called true patience.

Even if one's body were to be dismembered, limb by limb, with each joint severed and scattered, the mind remains free from anger; regarding both affection and the body as being like a wall, to observe the body in this way is the practice of patience.
When one hears from afar the harsh words uttered by others, if one can endure them and does not relish what is said in those various expressions, this constitutes patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, if one directs the will toward all impurities yet the mind remains tranquil and free from the knots of sorrow, and the intellect is able to discern all syllables and characters, the mind then enters into patience. Calculating that the path of patience is likewise, and that body, speech, and mind are all identical therein, it is called the Path.

Regarding those who propagate the holy teaching and provide much encouragement and assistance—whether their diligence be supreme, subtle, or intermediate—it is impossible to find the like of them even by gathering [merit] for billions of eons until they reach accomplishment.

If one exerts diligence such that nothing can be attained, and even when reckoning the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*), there is no acquisition, nor does one grasp at any phenomena (*dharma*), this is called diligence.

If the diligence one cultivates is such as this—free from cowardice and devoid of fear—it is termed the supreme, great, and penetrating diligence of a courageous and valiant Bodhisattva, fully endowed with benevolence and righteousness.
Thereupon the youth spoke again in verse:
"What is called patience is that which is eloquently proclaimed by the mouth;
it is patience because of the meaning of emptiness within emptiness, such that patience is equal to the three periods of time."
To speak of patience regarding forms and appearances, It is formless and invisible;
if the mind is equanimous toward these, Only then is it called patience.
The nature of patience is empty and still, Yet it encounters the conditions of sound, fragrance, and flavor.
That which is without words or letters is what is called patience.
To proclaim and teach these three types of patience— of body, speech, and mental intention—
if one understands them clearly, this is what is called the full realization of patience.
Though his body is dismembered limb by limb, his mind harbors no resentment;
his physical frame remains as unyielding as a wall—this is patience of the body.
Hearing evil words from afar, he does not retaliate with insults.
Entering this sound is patience; one is able to abide entirely within what is taught.
If, regarding all defects, the mind harbors no bonds of attachment, and if one can comprehend that syllables are empty, this mind enters into patience.
As with patience, so it is with the path; such are the actions of body, speech, and mind—this is what is called the "path," and it is that which is praised and assisted.
Whatever forms of diligence there may be—whether supreme, middling, or inferior—[they are likewise the path].
Even if one were to gather [merit] for billions of kalpas, one would not achieve success.
If diligence cannot be grasped, and the Way likewise yields nothing,
and one does not grasp at any dharma— this is called diligence.
"If one practices this with diligent effort, without timidity or harboring difficulties,
such a person is one of great vigor and a courageous Bodhisattva.
The youth further addressed those gathered in the assembly:

"What is called meditative concentration (dhyāna) is also without recollection; even in calculating [the nature of] dhyāna, there is no abiding. To abandon all conceptualizations—this is what is called the perfection of tranquility (śamatha-pāramitā)."

Thus, one is able to be tranquil and serene, remaining wordless and free from negligence; having abandoned all outflows (*āsrava*), one incinerates all defilements (*rajas*). This is called the perfection of tranquility (*śamatha-pāramitā*).
When the mind does not send forth or return toward any phenomena, and when the mind is detached from the mind, this is called the perfection of tranquility (śamatha-pāramitā).

When the mind and meditative concentration always reach the intention for the Way, and one constantly observes all these matters with equanimity—if one can thus maintain equanimity, there will be neither the deviant nor the correct within all that is observed; this is what is meant by saying that the Buddha-way is not difficult to attain.
To have no words and nothing spoken, to be neither exhaustible nor existent, to be without negligence and without self-indulgence—this is called the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).

There is no such limit as not crossing over to the other shore; furthermore, one abides in neither this nor that. One correctly establishes the dharma-realm by means of non-abiding, being without attachment and without words; there is nothing to be proclaimed, for there are no words!
No longer giving rise to any conceptualized thoughts, if one can open themselves to receive this Dharma, it is then called the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).

The other six perfections are likewise thus. If there is a person who contemplates this meaning equally, they will be able to bring all dharmas into equilibrium and will also be equal toward all sentient beings. If one can accord with all dharmas as they are, then one can bring all sentient beings into equilibrium; if one can bring all sentient beings into equilibrium, then one can bring all Buddhas into equality.
Having thus awakened to all Buddhas, one is then able to reverently cultivate all-knowledge; therefore, the bodhisattva is courageous and fearless, and for this reason it is called "infinite wisdom."
"If one can comply with and follow these instructions, then one follows the inconceivable Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, the youth spoke in verse:
"In the practice of dhyāna there is no thought; With single-minded focus, there is no dwelling."
Severing all conceptualizations is called the perfection of tranquility (*śamatha-pāramitā*).
Being serene and detached, free from dissipation and devoid of outflows (*āsrava*),
casting off all worldly toil— this is the perfection of tranquility.
Regarding the mind and all phenomena, it has never sent them back and forth;
with no-mind, it is liberated from the mind, silently crossing to the other shore.
When one reckons the mind and the Way, observing them both, they are entirely equal.
If one can discern equality, the Buddha-way is not difficult to attain.
Abandoning words and letters, there is no basis and nothing possessed;
neither delighting in nor being self-indulgent—this is what is called wisdom.
Without this, one does not cross to the other shore;
Not dwelling at the limits of this or that, one stands upright within the dharma-realm, Not dwelling in non-attachment.
There are no words to proclaim, Nor is there association with any conceptualization.
Receiving all dharmas through this is what is called wisdom.
Such is the nature of the perfections (pāramitās): when what is seen is of one kind, one can then equalize all dharmas and treat all sentient beings with impartiality.
Because they can equalize all phenomena, they can equalize sentient beings;
by being equal toward all phenomena, they are equal toward omniscience.
Therefore, with great wisdom, the bodhisattva is truly courageous.
"Those who can follow these instructions possess a Dharma-eye that is inconceivable.

When those noble beings had spoken these verses and analyzed their meaning, one thousand two hundred people all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, and sixty thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that time, the bodhisattvas seated upon the lotuses immediately descended, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, and further paid homage to the Bodhisattva Silent Speech. Together they addressed the Bodhisattva Silent Speech, saying:
"We have repaid the kindness of our holy teacher by revering and delighting in the True Dharma, serving the scriptures, and practicing filial piety with gratitude."
The venerable Śāriputra stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
For what reason do these bodhisattvas proclaim with their own mouths the words of the Tathāgata?”
"We are filial and grateful.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"These bodhisattvas have all been exhorted and inspired by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Aśabdaka (The Wordless One), who caused them to proclaim the teachings of the Way, to manifest kindness, compassion, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and ritual; and to expound the unsurpassed, true, and correct Mahāyāna teaching, transforming those who have not yet heard it so that they may resolve to attain the Way. This is what is meant by being filial and grateful."

To repay the kindness of my teacher, I have now come specifically to perform this offering; furthermore, I wish to behold this great assembly, to pay homage to the Buddha, and to listen to and study the scriptures so as to receive the teachings I have heard.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Avāca addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I wish to inquire of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha regarding the doubts and entanglements that trouble me; if I am granted permission, I shall venture to speak.”
The World-Honored One then addressed the Bodhisattva Silence:
"Ask whatever you wish regarding those things you do not understand; the Tathāgata shall explain each one for you, gladdening your heart so that no further doubts remain."
Then Śāriputra said to the Bodhisattva Silence:
"Noble son, since you are unable to speak, how do you wish to inquire about the meaning of the Tathāgata?"
Wu Yan replied:
"All methods of speech are entirely without characters and without words. Why is this so? Because..."
All sentient beings are entirely spontaneous, devoid of verbal teachings and manifold conceptualizations. O Śāriputra!
It is because of what the mind conceives that speech and words are uttered; if there were nothing conceived, there would be nothing spoken.
That which the mind contemplates is entirely empty and without reality; it cannot be spoken, it cannot be shown to others, nor can one inquire about its practice or contemplation.
Those who conceive of attachments find that they possess nothing at all, for there are no words [to describe them].
That which is empty and non-existent is likewise devoid of conceptualization and does not proclaim the discourse of written words.
Those who possess mindfulness of all conditioned phenomena do not conceive of themselves, saying:
"I shall proclaim the discourse of written words."
"One should not dwell on words, but practice with mindfulness and eloquently explain them through words. O Śāriputra!
The twelve links of dependent origination are profound and difficult to fathom; they are so sublime that what is produced by causes and conditions is itself spontaneous and ultimately non-existent."
If all things were naturally non-existent, then there would be no one who attains the realization of the Way. O Śāriputra!

All dharmas lack any causal basis for their formation; they are produced by depending on non-abiding, arising from the conjunction of conditions. Therefore, causes and conditions have no established foundation.

"O Śāriputra! All dharmas are entirely without a master, and even their sovereign rulers have no permanent master. They possess no volition; rather, due to one's own conceptualizations, they race about in many directions. From these oppositions, mindfulness arises, abiding amidst manifold perceptions, and from them, the faction of perversions is produced."

If someone were to ask him, or if one who sees him were to pose a difficult question, regarding whatever they might conceive or know—all these phenomena, whether with perception or without perception, are of a single characteristic, namely: the absence of perception.
The reason he asks this is that it constitutes the bodhisattva’s practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Śāriputra, it is for this reason that I have given rise to great compassion and questioned the Tathāgata; I do not inquire about matters through mere words or sounds, nor do I rely on oral instruction, but rather ask as a bodhisattva established in great compassion.
Śāriputra asked:
"If there are no sentient beings, no persons, and no things, for what reason does a bodhisattva give rise to great compassion toward sentient beings?"
Wu-yen replied: "O Śāriputra!
If sentient beings did not seek to achieve realization and reach the Way, then the Bodhisattva would not give rise to great compassion for them."

However, among sentient beings, there is no sentient being who gives rise to the notion of a "sentient being"; for this reason, the Bodhisattva dwells among sentient beings and arouses great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
To speak of there being a person would be contrary to reality, for all five destinies are like illusions and transformations.
Alas, how painful! These people are inverted;
they lack the notion of a sentient being. Therefore, for their sake, I preach the Way of the Sūtras, so that they may realize that there is no self and that both beginning and end are empty.

For this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for all sentient beings; he does not cause destruction, nor does he destroy anything that exists, nor does he destroy the self, others, or the life-span. Therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattva enters into great compassion to guide and benefit sentient beings.

Seeing that the nature of emptiness is clearly discerned as it truly is, yet is defiled by adventitious dust, and observing that while one may enter into all forms, they are seen by oneself to be fundamentally and entirely pure—for this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings.
At that time, Śāriputra praised the Bodhisattva Silent Speech, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
It is exactly as you have said, without any difference.
Furthermore, having heard the eloquence with which the Venerable One just now spoke, I wish to pose a question; I shall receive such an inconceivable teaching from this True Being.

Regarding the Dharma that has been proclaimed and the questions posed therein, I shall ensure that the evil Māras find no opportunity, so that the Tathāgata’s Dharma may endure for a long time. Furthermore, let this assembly—consisting of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, both human and non-human—attain the immeasurable radiance of the path of the Dharma.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Avacana came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you have often said that there are two causes and conditions for one who cultivates right view:
hearing the sound from another and reflecting upon its practice.”
Excellent!
Great Sage!
We pray only that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will analyze and proclaim it.
What is meant by a bodhisattva receiving the sounds of others?
What is meant by reflection?
And what is the right view of the noble ones?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avākya:
“Noble son! Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall now explain it in detail.”
"It is just as a bodhisattva, receiving the sounds of others, reflects upon them and thus accords with the right view of the noble ones. "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
Thus, Bodhisattva Wordless and the great assembly received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
“O son of good family!
If there is a bodhisattva who exhorts and transforms sentient beings to enter the Buddha-way, this is for the bodhisattva to rely upon the voices of others;
if that person’s mind remains free from distraction, this is what constitutes reflection.”
If one contemplates the intention for the Path with equanimity, this constitutes the right view of the noble ones.
Furthermore, if one listens to and examines the gentle and compliant Dharma, this is "receiving the voice of another";
if one can uphold the meaning of the Buddha's Path, this is "reflection."
If one can practice the path of a bodhisattva and attain the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), this constitutes the right view of the noble ones.
Furthermore, Wordless One!

If one can proclaim the subtle wisdom heard from others—the unsurpassed, true, and correct—and by relying upon these sounds from others, is able to penetrate them without conceiving of a self, this constitutes reflection.
To have a nature of pure resolve, free from flattery and deceit, and to initiate great undertakings—this is the right view of the noble ones.
To hear teachings that accord with the meaning and do not contradict the Dharma is to rely on the voices of others;
to cultivate the roots of all virtues is what constitutes contemplation.
To practice with subtlety and encourage others toward the Path—this is the right view of the noble ones.
To listen and receive with single-minded diligence is to follow the voice of another;
to seek out extraordinary meanings is to engage in reflection.
To never forget or abandon the aspiration for the Way (bodhicitta) through encouragement is the right view of the noble ones (ārya).

To mindfully accord with what is appropriate to encourage the aspiration for the Way, never falling back from the equanimous contemplation of the noble ones, and to relinquish all that is heard or thought of, is to rely on the voice of others.
To be able to give away everything worthy of respect without any sense of attachment or stinginess is what constitutes reflection (cintā).
To have no expectation of reward and no greedy attachment even toward the Way, reaching thus unto the Mahāyāna—this is the right view of the worthy and holy.
Hearing the profound and elegant teachings of the prohibitions and precepts is "receiving the voice of another";
that the mind which upholds the precepts neither clings to nor abandons anything is "reflection."
To have no [deluded] conduct regarding the precepts, to possess firm faith in the ultimate truth, and to exhort and assist others toward the Way—this is the right view of the worthy and noble.
To listen, examine, and practice patience, benevolence, righteousness, and great compassion is to receive the sounds of others;
yet to harbor a mind of pity and sympathy without any intent to harm is what constitutes reflection.
Ultimate tranquility consists in believing that all dharmas exhaustively assist the path to Buddhahood; this is the right view of the noble ones.
To listen, examine, and apply oneself with diligence in accordance with this is to rely on the voices of others;
for the mind to dwell neither in indolence nor in defilement is what constitutes reflection.
To be without conjunction or dispersion, without transgression or loss, and to diligently apply oneself with vigor to encourage and assist the Path—this is the right view of the noble ones.
To hear of the gates of dhyāna-concentration and the three doors of liberation, as well as samādhi and correct reception (samāpatti), is to rely on the voices of others.
That which is performed by the mind cannot be apprehended; to observe the fundamental nature of the mind is what constitutes reflection.
To cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) without falling into inversion and to encourage and assist the Buddha-way—this is the right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) of the noble ones (*ārya*).
To hear and listen to wisdom so that the roots, flowers, and fruits of the body are perfected—this is relying on the voice of others (*parato ghoṣa*).
To observe the beginning, end, and ultimate destination of the Dharma one has heard—this is reflection (*cintā*).
To cast aside all currents and abandon the depths and sources of the various precipices in order to open the way for transformation is the correct vision of the worthy and sages.
To demonstrate the four debts of gratitude, to listen to and gather what is heard while remaining entirely free from attachment—this is receiving the voice of another;
never to neglect or abandon the teaching of the four debts of gratitude is what constitutes reflection.

That which provides salvation extends its grace to all sentient beings; this is the principle of equality. To establish them in omniscience through liberation is the right view of the worthy and the sage.
To cultivate the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—is to rely on the voices of others.
To not destroy or abandon the compassionate love for all classes of beings, nor to disparage them; to practice what one follows without seeking fame or reputation—this is reflection.

To take delight in emptiness and non-existence, yet to cultivate pity and sorrow for the sake of sentient beings; to practice joy for the sake of the Dharma; and to encourage and assist in the Way for the sake of the two rewards (present and future)—this is the right view of the noble ones.
If one listens to and examines the fourfold analytical eloquence, this is "hearing from others" (parato ghoṣa).
To observe the majestic deportment and ritual propriety of all dharmas is "reflection" (cintā).
To attain equanimity regarding the meaning of the Dharma and to fulfill one's practice by inspiring the aspiration for the Path—this is the right view of the noble ones (ārya-samyag-dṛṣṭi).
If one hears the subtle and beneficial matters that ought to be practiced and followed, this is "receiving the voice of another" (śrutamaya-jñāna).
To mindfully govern and practice them without departing from them is "reflection" (cintāmaya-jñāna).
As for the chapters and verses, the tracks of the Path, and the places from which the Buddha-way is proclaimed, these constitute the "right view" (samyagdṛṣṭi) of the noble ones.
If one can cause others to hear the Dharma of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, this is "receiving the voice of another.

Cultivating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) without any confusion, practicing the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), never being deluded by following unwholesome thoughts, and always conforming to the will toward virtue and righteousness; as for the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), exerting diligence and meditative concentration without harboring cowardice, having firm faith in this way, clearly understanding the chapters and verses without retreating, and using wisdom to seek out and respond while observing each thing individually; when the mind, through these powers, does not engage in worldly defilements and enters the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) equal to the mind of the Path—this is called "contemplation" (*cintā*).

If one is without intention and without mental preoccupation, such that the four foundations of mindfulness neither arise nor cease; if one makes the body and mind supple through the four right efforts; if one examines the four bases of psychic power according to the true reality; if one understands things in this way and proceeds accordingly—wielding the sword of wisdom to sever all defilements, so that the passions do not scatter but enter into the True Dharma; and if, regarding the factors of enlightenment, one descends into equal contemplation where there are no two separate things—then this path of return, which encourages and assists the mind toward the Way, constitutes the right view of the noble ones.
If one hears and listens to the Four Noble Truths, this is "receiving the voice of another.

To contemplate the suffering and affliction of the five aggregates, the hardships of affection and love, and the exhaustion of the retribution of habitual causes and conditions, thereby entering the path—this is "reflection.

Although dwelling amidst all sufferings, wisdom does not arise; regarding all that is habitually practiced, wisdom does not practice; regarding all that is extinguished, wisdom is ultimately exhausted; and because wisdom regarding the path is without attachment, it inspires the Great Way—this is the Right View of the noble ones.
If one listens to and receives the three gates of liberation, this is "hearing the voice of another.
To have profound faith in emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without fear of the signless (*animitta*), and to have no aspiration for the wishless (*apraṇihita*), is "reflection.

Not giving rise to the practice of emptiness while transforming various views, initiating the signless to instruct all beings, and causing all practices of signs to arise from the wishless—such sincerity as this is the right view of the noble ones (*ārya*).
To cause those who have first resolved their minds to accord with and follow the Great Enterprise is "receiving the voice of others";
to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva without abandoning anything is "reflection";
and to attain perfect enlightenment upon reaching the stage of non-retrogression is the "right view of the noble ones."
To encounter a virtuous friend and follow their instructions is "receiving the voice of others";
to see the World-Honored One with one's own eyes and receive instruction on the noble path is "reflection";
to act in accordance with what one says, such that body and speech are in harmony, is the right view of the noble ones.
Hearing the Dharma being expounded as being equivalent to a delusion is "receiving the voice of another";
observing the ultimate destination of the meaning of all dharmas is "reflection";
and practicing the meaning of the Dharma without losing the Way of the Teachings is the "right view of the noble ones."
To draw near to the Tathāgata and receive his teachings is "hearing from others";
to discern the path with consciousness and not abandon the Great Way is "reflection";
to accept and practice them so as to transform and bring others to fulfillment is the "right view of the noble ones."
To be able to hear and receive the eighty-four thousand dharmas of the path-factors is to rely on the voices of others;
to clearly understand and discern the eighty-four thousand practices of the Buddhas is contemplation;
and to preach the Dharma according to the needs of the eighty-four thousand classes of sentient beings with their various faculties is the right view of the noble ones.
To find no pleasure whatsoever in whatever one encounters, yet to give rise to a mind of merit—this is relying on the voices of others.
If that mind does not abandon merit, this is reflection.
To single-mindedly and diligently encourage all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) through this mind of merit—this is the right view of the noble ones (*ārya*).

"This son of good family, if he maintains mindfulness in accordance with reality, his life will be long and his lifespan immeasurable, without beginning or end, characterized by the right view of the noble ones. Why is this so?

The cycling through the five destinies is like an illusion, a transformation, a dream, a shadow, an echo, a mirage, the moon in water, or a plantain tree; to understand them thus is to rely upon the voice of others.
That all phenomena are entirely equal and without partiality or deviation is what constitutes reflection.
To attain such equality is the right view of the noble ones.

It is called "contemplation": neither elevating nor depressing; regarding all phenomena, there is neither conformity nor non-conformity, neither progress nor non-progress, neither abiding nor non-abiding, neither practice nor non-practice, neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness, neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization, neither intentionality nor non-intentionality, neither contemplation nor non-contemplation, and no mental instruction—this is what is called the Dharma-gate of Entering Non-duality.
Having realized this single category, there is no conjunction and no dispersion, no opposition and no compliance.

Having realized that the nature of profound mindfulness is fundamentally pure, one should preach it as being supremely radiant; therein is neither darkness nor light, neither turbidity nor clarity, and no hierarchical gradations—it is the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), indestructible and unmoving within the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi).

Entering into the rootless, they abide in the three periods of time without abiding anywhere; there is no self, no person, no life-span, no vital principle, no sound, and no voice. They treat all syllables as equal, finding no objective referent in their meaning; they possess no wealth or karma, and have nothing to be established or set aside. Having attained the exhaustion of all things, they are free from all discursive thoughts regarding any practice.

Free from all conceptualizations, having completely severed all matters of negligence, and having extinguished all modes of mental activity, they are without attachment and relinquish all that is clung to—lofty indeed, reaching even to what is praised by the Tathāgata!

The unconditioned practice consists in cutting away all discursive thoughts; this is what constitutes equanimity. One should contemplate that which is formless and uniform as being suchness (*tathatā*).

Even if a practitioner arises from samādhi, they should explain this Dharma to sentient beings and others, seeking its fundamental source therein. Contemplating it as it truly is, they treat it accordingly, remaining unshakable; this is called "establishing oneself in great compassion and the right view of the noble ones."
When the Buddha spoke on the noble and holy right view, ten thousand bodhisattvas immediately attained noble and holy right view.
Thereupon, Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Aśabdaka:
“O son of good family!
"From whom did you hear the Dharma such that you are able to give rise to this noble and holy right view?
Wuyanyan replied, "O Śāriputra!..."
The Dharma from which I have heard is unconditioned; it does not lead to the Path through a mind of the past, nor through the future, nor through the present.

It is equal across the three periods of time and equalizes all dharmas. For those who pursue any destination, there is no place of return; there is neither dharma, nor is there anything to be equalized.
It is from that [state] that I have heard the Dharma.

Neither conditioned nor unconditioned, without consciousness, without abiding, and without mind or mental consciousness, one should not hold to anything among all phenomena; one restrains the minds of all sentient beings, bringing joy to all people, yet finds no gain in meaning and remains unshakable, remaining unattached even to the poison of powerlessness;
it was from him that I truly heard the Dharma.
I see that those born into the world are neither born nor arisen; if all phenomena do not originate, they are without basis for conceptualization and are ineffable;
it is from this very perspective that I have heard the Dharma.

Abiding in the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), he equally governs the realm of persons (*pudgaladhātu*); the realm of phenomena, the realm of persons, and the realm of space are not differentiated. All realms are equal and unarisen, without the fabrication of manifoldness;
it is from him that I have correctly heard the Dharma.

He does not dwell in a bodhimaṇḍa, nor sit beneath a tree, nor engage in walking meditation; he neither attains Buddhahood nor relies upon the Path, nor does he abandon the mundane world, so as not to cause those people who are attached to give rise to such thoughts.

The Tathāgata attains the Way yet does not attain the Way; he attains the primary and secondary marks yet does not attain marks; he realizes realization yet does not realize it—all of which proceeds from the nature of original purity and spontaneity.

"O Śāriputra! The Dharma is without support; because it cannot be grasped, it has no body. Because it has no body, there is nothing accomplished. Because there is nothing accomplished, there is no arising. Because there is no arising, there is no origination. Because there is no origination, there is no passing away. Because there is no passing away, there is no attachment. Because there is no attachment, there is no wavering. Because there is no wavering, there is no activity. Because there is no activity, one flows with the swift current."
Having already navigated the swift waters, one has nothing further to attain; having attained nothing, the body crosses to the other shore.
Having crossed to the other shore, there is no sinking; where there is no sinking, there is no vessel. Where there is no vessel, there is nothing to which one should respond;
where there is nothing to which one should respond, one is free from craving and desire. Being free from craving and desire, there is no conceptualization. Having [attained this]...
When there is no conceptualization, all disturbances are severed; once all disturbances are severed, one’s fundamental nature is pure.
Through this purity, there is no defilement; with no defilement, there is no worldly affliction (*kleśa*). With no worldly affliction, there is no semblance of identity;
because there is no semblance of identity, one abides in equanimity. By abiding in fundamental equanimity, one is established.
It is immovable; by establishing immovability, there is nothing sought; because there is nothing sought, it is like the ultimate truth (*tattva*);
being like the ultimate truth, it is like thorough reality; because it is like thorough reality, there is nothing that exists;
because there is nothing that exists, there is no objectification toward any conditions (*pratyaya*); and for one who has no objectification toward any conditions—
Thus, one transcends the spheres; by transcending the spheres, that which arises in all realms neither arises nor ceases.
Because there is nothing raised up, there is nothing lowered down. Because there is nothing lowered down, there is no gateway. Because there is no gateway, one is free from verbal instruction.
Because one is free from verbal instruction, one transcends the categories of consciousness. Because one transcends the categories of consciousness, one does not...
Returning again, because there is no returning, there is no place; because there is no place, there is no non-place;
because there is no non-place, there is no seed-grain; because there is no seed-grain, there is no root or sprout;
because there is no root or sprout, there is no conditioned activity. Thus one transcends the traces of all consciousnesses, becoming tranquil and still, reaching the ultimate state.
It is tranquil and ultimately serene; having reached serenity, one reaches the state of non-contemplation (*avitarka*). Through non-contemplation, one ultimately reaches freedom from resentment;
having reached freedom from resentment, one reaches the realization of the mind’s intent. Having reached the realization of the mind’s intent, it no longer arises again;
because it does not arise again, one returns to the Way of equality and non-action—this is the Dharma.
"O Śāriputra! Such is the nature of the Dharma;
when a sutra is taught in this manner, what kind of person is one who possesses right view?"

As for that right view, it is equal to one's own body; by being equal to one's own body, one is free from conjunction and meeting. Being free from conjunction and meeting, one does not perceive equality within all things that are equal, and regarding all that is seen, it is as if there were no conceptualization.
“Śāriputra, this is the proclamation of the Dharma and Vinaya, the right view of the noble ones.
Bodhisattva Silence said to Śāriputra:

“Just as one regards the attachments of ignorance and craving as equal, so too does one regard the matters of wisdom, clarity, and liberation as equal; being equal toward nirvāṇa, neither acting nor refraining from acting—this is the attainment of the right view of the noble ones.”
If, upon whatever one perceives, one does not grasp at divergent views, this is the right view of the noble ones!
Furthermore, Śāriputra, consider this:

If one can be equal toward lust, anger, and ignorance, and likewise equal toward emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the characteristics of liberation—then these constitute a single characteristic, namely, the return to signlessness.
To be able to take refuge in this matter of equality is the right view of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Furthermore, one who abides in right view does not create dualistic phenomena regarding all things that are equal; being free from dualistic phenomena, they do not dwell in association (*saṃprayoga*); being free from association, they have no place of abiding. Thus, they attain the universal equality of all phenomena without distinction—this is the right view of the noble ones.
Furthermore, that which is equal and non-dual is equal to sentient beings, equal to all Buddhas, and equal to all dharmas.

Being equal to all dharmas, one is equal to the buddha-fields; being equal to the buddha-fields, one is equal to empty space. If one does not shift from this equality and can abide in this equanimity, practicing without a fixed dwelling place—this is the right view of the noble ones.
Therefore, Śāriputra, as is the nature of the Dharma, so too is the listener; right view is thus.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:
Has the Elder aroused right view?
From whom did you hear the Dharma?
What is the nature of what you have seen?
Śāriputra replied:
"O son of good family! As for me now, having heard the Dharma you have taught and examined its essential meaning, I find that whatever I might speak would all fall short and be deficient."
Wu Yan replied: "So it is, so it is! Śāriputra!"
"Whatever words I venture to speak, they are all deficient and lacking.
Śāriputra asked again: "Noble son!"
“The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, possesses an immeasurable assembly of merit through which he proclaims his teachings; how could that which he speaks fall short or be deficient?
Wuyuan replied, “To speak in such a manner is to have nothing at all to say; thus, it does not fall short or become deficient.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata, the Arhat, does not give rise to fame or virtue; one should not long for the supreme blessings of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
That Tathāgata has no virtue and no appellation.
As for the meaning of "Tathāgata," there is no origin; the Tathāgata is likewise thus, abiding in the unoriginated without moving or shifting.

If there are those who do not desire the supreme virtues of the Tathāgata, that which they admire will lack equanimity; furthermore, they will harbor partiality and deviance regarding both desire and desirelessness. Those who possess such admiration fall into deficiency and deprivation.
Śāriputra asked:
"O son of noble family!
What is meant by being without deficiency or lack regarding the Dharma?"

Wu Yan replied: "There are no great things, no five aggregates, and no six sense bases; one does not receive them upon the crown of the head, there is nothing to be summoned, and there is nothing at all to be practiced. There are no words, neither instruction nor non-instruction; thus, regarding the Dharma of the Path, one ensures that mind, intellect, and consciousness do not arise. This Dharma is without deficiency;
if one were to give rise to mind, intellect, and consciousness, one would fall into deficiency."
If one regards phenomena as having activity or non-activity, one falls into deficiency;
if one regards phenomena as neither active nor inactive, then there is no deficiency.
Furthermore, if one discriminates among phenomena, eliminates them, practices them, or realizes them, one falls into deficiency.
If there is no clear understanding and no removal of what is to be discarded, nor any practice, nor the realization of attainment, then there is no deficiency.
If one perceives something while having nothing to hear or explain, yet teaches and attains a cognitive awareness of the destination, then one falls into deficiency;
if one does not engage in any realm whatsoever, then there is no deficiency.
If one perceives either merit or faults, one falls into deficiency;
however, if one’s conduct is free from faults, and there is neither the reputation for virtue nor any perception at all, then there is no deficiency.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Silent Speech:
“Excellent, excellent,
son of good family!”
"If you wish to preach the Dharma, you should speak in this manner.
At that time, twelve thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Bodhisattva Silence (*Avākya*) again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I recall that the Tathāgata expounded the four powers for the sake of the bodhisattvas: first, the power of faith; second, the power of diligence; third, the power of intention; and fourth, the power of wisdom.”
Only the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, extensively analyzes and explains these four kinds of power.
What are the bodhisattva’s powers of resolute faith, diligence, intention, and wisdom?
The Buddha said to Bodhisattva Anabhilāpya:
“Listen attentively and reflect well!
“Excellent! [he replied.]
“World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Wordless received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: "Noble son!
If a bodhisattva believes in all the Buddha-dharmas, cherishing them with joy and compliance, harboring no doubt and having no hesitation, this is the power of faith."

When the Buddhas first sought the Way through their diligence, they aspired to this scripture without negligence or abandonment; they harbored no cowardice nor did they regress—this is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).

If they restrain their resolve and gather the roots of virtue without forgetfulness, with an undisturbed mind that does not forsake the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), and by means of a truly upright mind that encourages and assists the Way regardless of whether things arise or cease—this is the power of intention (*cetanā-bala*).

As for the wisdom they cultivate, it is luminous regarding all phenomena; attaining mastery without depending on the wisdom of others, their insight is unimpeded—this is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Aśabdaka:
"To have faith in the noble ones and to walk alone through the triple world without doubt or difficulty—this is the power of faith.
To practice giving with diligence and to reverently accord with the teachings—this is the power of vigor."
That which the mind contemplates is to constantly reflect upon what has been proclaimed by the worthy and noble ones, never forgetting or abandoning it; this is the power of intention (*manas-bala*).
If one hears the fundamental wisdom scriptures from the Most Holy One and is able to practice them accordingly, this is the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*).
Furthermore, if one has profound faith in the retribution of sin and merit without doubt or confusion, this is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*);
if one can diligently practice what should be done and refrain from doing what should not be done, this is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*);
if one maintains mindfulness so that the karmic actions initiated never decay, this is the power of intention (*citta-bala*).
"If one can clearly understand that there is no retribution for sin or merit, and is able to discern all dharmas, this is the power of wisdom.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Wu-yen:
"If one's mind is pure and stainless, and is able to restrain the will so as to accord with the teachings of the Way, this is the power of faith."
To receive what the mind has been inspired to accept and to nurture it is the power of diligence;
to cause the mind to always accord with its intent and remain one-pointed is the power of volition;
and for the mind to contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions is the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, to have faith that all phenomena are entirely empty is the power of faith;
to cultivate diligence so as to liberate oneself from the bonds of various views is the power of diligence;
and to harbor no fear regarding internal and external emptiness is the power of mind.
To contemplate ultimate emptiness such that both the beginning and the end are entirely empty is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
To be without signs (*animitta*) and without aspiration (*apraṇihita*) regarding all phenomena, and to perform no conditioned activity, is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*);
to use these dharmas of the Path to analyze and explain them for others is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).
If one maintains mindfulness regarding all phenomena and acts with composure, this is the power of the mind (*manobala*).

As for that which was previously taught and is now being proclaimed and disseminated, if one thoroughly searches for it and finds it to be ultimately ungraspable, this is the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*).
One should reflect within one's own mind regarding all things: to desire to relinquish them through the sphere of faith and generosity is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).

To relinquish without harboring weariness, never being timid or inferior toward the Great Way, never deviating from it, and practicing giving and bestowing while also encouraging others toward the aspiration for the Way—this is the power of intention (*cetanā-bala*).
To realize that there is neither a giver nor a recipient, and to not harbor expectations for karmic retribution—this is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*).
To respectfully follow the prohibitions and precepts, thereby accomplishing the fruit of true faith and morality, is the power of faith;
to use diligence to eliminate all thoughts of violating the precepts is the power of diligence;
and to maintain mindfulness of the honored prohibitions and precepts through the mind of the Way without forgetting, so as to assist toward all-knowledge (sarvajñā), is the power of intention.

To contemplate the body as a shadow, speech as an echo, and the mind as a magical illusion; to examine the prohibitive precepts without any [self-referential] activity—this is the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*).
To achieve patience and have faith in majestic power is the power of faith (*śraddhābala*).

As for the diligence in one's practice: not listening to various discursive thoughts, not uttering coarse words intended for others, and not following deviant paths—even if one’s limbs were to be dismembered and the flesh of one’s body cut away, one gathers the power of patience and never harbors anger, practicing patience with a heart of loving-kindness—this is the power of diligence (*vīryabala*).
To practice patience in order to encourage and assist toward all-knowledge is the power of the mind;
to be without body-consciousness and to find neither body nor mind is the power of wisdom.
The Path consists of diligence and not indolence; for one who has faith in this and whose mind is joyful, flourishing, and firmly convinced, this is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).

To constantly practice diligence without abandoning it for even a moment, to act without attachment while transforming sentient beings, to protect the True Dharma, to plant the roots of all virtues, to serve and make offerings to the Buddhas in accordance with their teachings—all for the sake of all sentient beings—and to cultivate and purify the adornments of Buddha-lands and the reputation of one’s name and virtue, is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).

To eliminate the defilements of anger and indolence in all sentient beings, and through the diligence cultivated by donning the armor of virtue to encourage and assist toward all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), is the power of intention (*citta-bala*).

If one does not harbor earnest delusions regarding the Path, yet does not lose the correctness of dignified demeanor and ritual propriety, and through discerning diligence fails to find any fixed location for all dharmas—this is the power of wisdom.
To delight in dwelling in seclusion, in quietude, and in solitude, without longing for assemblies and instead giving rise to the power of joy—this is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).

To practice diligence in one’s conduct, to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and to give rise to the doors of liberation, samādhis, and right reception (*samāpatti*)—this is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).
To remain unshakable due to the causes and conditions through which one attains meditative reflection—this is the power of intention (*citta-bala*).

Within that single-minded state, one contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, without distracting the dhyāna, without disparaging the dhyāna, and without regressing from the dhyāna; clearly understanding skillful means (*upāya*) and employing them appropriately as the situation requires—this is called using skillful means to guide, encourage, and lead others toward the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*).
To hear all the dharmas of the various pāramitās and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), and if one can believe in them, this is the power of faith (śraddhā-bala).

To retain everything heard without forgetting, to be able to praise the skillful means for others and establish them in those dharmas—whether they follow them or do not follow them—to examine their own beginning and end, this is the power of diligence (vīrya-bala).
To abide among sentient beings with an undisturbed mind, moving amidst desire and attachment like a lotus flower, and to transform and teach all, this is the power of intention (citta-bala).

To examine that the three realms are empty—like foam, a plantain tree, a mirage, a shadow, an echo, an illusion, and a transformation—and to reveal what has not been heard before, is the power of wisdom.
To direct a clear and pure mind toward sentient beings with compassion that is all-pervasive is the power of faith;
to believe in great compassion and to ensure that whatever the mind undertakes is never indolent is the power of diligence;
to delight in the correct scriptures, not forsake the joy of the Dharma, and constantly uphold and practice them is the power of intention.

The mind being unattached and harboring no malice, not creating duality, neither advancing nor retreating, and attaining tranquil contemplation while practicing the True Dharma—this is the power of wisdom.

Reflecting upon the human body—that it cannot endure for long due to the power of countless evils, defects, impurities, and chaos; that one merely provides sustenance for this stubborn serpent; and that all this arises from deviant conduct—to understand things thus is the power of faith (*śraddhā-bala*).

If one quickly sinks into the calamities of suffering and manifold afflictions arrive together, realizing that this is the very nature of birth and death, and observing the Buddha-dharma, this is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).

Even if the mind changes toward what is unwholesome or refuses to comply, the mind does not follow the paths of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; furthermore, the mind does not follow worldly desires, greed, or envy, nor does it follow broken precepts or evil wisdom—this is the power of the mind (*citta-bala*).

If one enters the category of wisdom that discerns the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmaprajñā*), enters the wisdom that elucidates and comprehends the essence, and possesses the wisdom of the past, future, and present, this is called the power of wisdom (*jñānabala*).

Joy is the characteristic of faith; non-retrogression is the characteristic of diligence; contemplation is the characteristic of intention; and clear comprehension is the characteristic of wisdom. One practices the power of faith, does not abandon the power of diligence, does not lose the power of intention, and cultivates the power of wisdom.
To preach the Dharma for others according to their ailments and administer the appropriate medicine; to clearly understand all hindrances is called "faith";
to transcend all hindrances is called "diligence";
and to have no further attachments is called "mind."
To thoroughly understand hindrances is wisdom.
To delight in the Buddha-dharma and give rise to profound faith, and through the arising of that profound faith to generate the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta), is the power of faith.
To respectfully cultivate various practices and accumulate the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) is the power of diligence.
The patient acceptance of the dharma of pliancy is the power of the mind;
if one attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, that is the power of wisdom.
Faith as a faculty constitutes patience, which is the power of the mind.
If one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this constitutes the power of wisdom.
The faculty of faith becomes the power of faith;
the faculty of vigor becomes the power of diligence.
"The faculty of mind is the power of the mind;
through meditative contemplation one subdues the faculties, and the Great Sage penetrates the faculties, reaching everywhere without exception—this is the power of wisdom.

When the Buddha spoke these words, eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and forty-two thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
The Sutra of the Silent Youth, Volume One;
The Sutra of the Silent Youth Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Padmaviśuddha who asked the Bodhisattva Anabhilāpya:

"Noble son, when you have conceived this intention and questioned the Tathāgata, will you receive an answer and explanation regarding subtle and wondrous practices, such that you may be delighted in heart as if receiving the dyeing of the Dharma?"
Wu-yen replied: "O son of noble family!
Since the very beginning, I have never inquired after the Dharma, nor have I received it. By what cause, then, could there be the defilement of the Dharma that might defile my mind?"
He said: "Noble son!
Have you not, as a virtuous person, ever heard and received the Dharma from the Tathāgata?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"Why? He replied, "Because he is not a fit vessel."
He asked again,
"Are you not a fit vessel for expounding the Dharma?
He replied:
"So it is! He asked again:
"What is your vessel, O Venerable One?"
He replied, "Regarding the categories of all dharmas, I am not a fit vessel; there is nothing further extraordinary about me.
He asked again:
“Noble son! If one is not a fit vessel, by what cause could they ever attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment?
He replied:
"The Way is not that which serves as a vessel for the Dharma.
He asked again:
"Is one who examines the Way not a vessel for the Buddha-Dharma?"
He replied:
"If that path were separate from the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-dharma would not be its vessel; yet that path is not separate from the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, because one reckons the Buddha-dharma as being this very path, and that path as being the Buddha-dharma."
O son of good family!

I do not wish for the Dharma of the Buddhas to be separated from worldly toil, nor for one to constantly lack resolve for the Way; how much less could one delight in the Buddha-Dharma while remaining apart from the Way?

Why is this so? Those who possess the Buddha-dharma do not depart from worldly defilements (*kleśa*), and yet those defilements do not depart from the Path; to fully awaken to and comprehend sensual desires is what is called the Path.

For this reason, I do not calculate "what is mine" nor do I differentiate between [this] and the Buddha-way; those with divergent intentions each calculate things as distinct, yet one should not seek the Way in disparate places.
"Suppose there were someone who sought these various distinctions in different places; yet, even if another person did not seek such distinctions, they would not be considered distinct.
He asked again:
"By what means are they distinguished?"
He replied:
"To say that the self (*ātman*) is distinct and not identical with the Path is called 'difference.

To say that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are different from the self, the person, or the life-span; that the mind and consciousness are different; and that lust, anger, and delusion are different—this is what is meant by 'difference.'"

If one can clearly understand that the self is naturally pure from beginning to end, and that the Way is naturally pure from beginning to end, then one may say there is no difference between the self, others, and the life-span; that lust, anger, and ignorance are naturally pure, and the Way is likewise naturally and ultimately pure—this is what is meant by "no difference."
If they were different, one could not seek them as different; thus, one should seek all dharmas within this body of the four great elements and within the self.

Seeking in this manner, one finds nothing to be obtained. If one creates attachment within that which is unobtainable, there is no place for such non-attachment. Where there is no attachment, there is no locus.

All dharmas are entirely without abiding and have no original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). If there is no original limit, that is the true original limit; because the true original limit has no limit of interruption, one does not calculate a future limit, nor is there a limited limit, nor a limitless limit. Such is the original limit of all dharmas.
If one enters this limit, there is neither thought nor non-thought; one is neither in birth-and-death nor in extinction, yet ultimately attains the extinction of all dharmas.
If one attains extinction through this dharma, one reaches tranquility and causes all who have not attained extinction to attain it.
As the World-Honored One said:

"One who cannot discipline oneself, who is not tranquil and liberated, and who does not follow the teaching to attain extinction, yet wishes to transform others so that they may attain extinction—such a thing has never existed."
"Being naturally tranquil and liberated in accordance with the discipline, one attains the crossing over to the unconditioned and is able to deliver those who have not yet crossed over.

These matters are as they have been described; this is the practice of a bodhisattva. If one wishes to attain the dharma of extinction (nirvāṇa), one must immediately cultivate the conduct of a bodhisattva; thus, one will be able to understand all conditioned phenomena and penetrate the characteristics of the dharma-realm.

A practitioner who acts in this way will be able to see the root of all virtues; their eyes will no longer behold the traces of the movements of the hosts of Māra’s officials, and they shall follow and cultivate this compendium of the Buddha-dharma without losing samādhi.
In this way, the practitioner transforms and enlightens sentient beings, proclaiming and elucidating all realms so that they transcend non-self.
In this way, the practitioner receives all dharmas, causing all afflictions to be naturally and completely eliminated.
Thus, although such a practitioner acts within the world, they do not cling to worldly conventions.
Thus, although such a practitioner maintains the five aggregates, they do not dwell in consciousness.
Thus, although such a practitioner experiences the four great elements, they stand firm within the dharma-realm without wavering.
In this way, the practitioner gathers all the sense bases (*āyatana*) and brings them to the gates of liberation.

In this way, the practitioner manifests the various realms (*dhātu*) as the *pāramitās*; walking alone upon the Great Way, they enter the triple world (*tridhātu*), manifesting worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) while remaining free from defilement.

Thus, when a practitioner practices the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), they do not conceive of it as a perfection, nor do they dwell anywhere; likewise, regarding morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, when practicing the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not conceive of it as wisdom, nor do they dwell anywhere.
A practitioner who acts in this way does not abandon any of the various practices; what they cultivate is thorough, definitive, and ultimately pure.
Such a practitioner cultivates the bodhisattva conduct, and the path they follow and practice is without differentiation.
One who practices the bodhisattva path is without duality; being without duality is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Practicing the bodhisattva path, one is without "I" or "mine," does not reckon in a self-body, and has no reception—this is the practice of a bodhisattva. One who cultivates this path is without obstruction; having eliminated all [worldly] blessings and abandonments, they become a bodhisattva.
"One who cultivates the Way does not suffer from harm; awakening to and discerning that there is neither meeting nor unconditioned activity—such a one is a bodhisattva.
He asked again:
"What is meant by being correctly designated as a bodhisattva?"
He replied: "It is for the sake of those who do not understand the meaning of the Way that one is called a 'bodhisattva.

By following the teachings of the Way, they give rise to tranquility and do not destroy the Buddha-dharma; they uphold the words of the Dharma to protect the assembly of sages. Thus, their resolve for the Way remains unshakable; their minds do not dwell upon the stages of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; they do not disturb their pure nature, nor do they utter words that are beyond designation."

This is the ultimate vow: to deliver those not yet delivered, to bring peace to those who are not at peace, to enable those who have not attained parinirvāṇa to attain it, and to embrace worldly afflictions without falling into desirelessness.

Contemplating that which is born from the unborn, one carefully observes emptiness; without seeking to save sentient beings, one observes signlessness and does not conceive attachment to the Path; practicing wishlessness, one arises in accordance with worldly convention.

Seeking the Buddha-body, one is not defiled by the various desires; observing conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), one awakens to their true nature, remaining neither lost nor deluded, thereby attaining worldly wisdom (*loka-prajñā*).
Wielding the weapons of wisdom, they subdue the thieves of the five aggregates and the calamities of the six sense-decays;
they transform pride and arrogance, bestowing upon themselves adornments and purifying the Buddha-lands. With the adornment of precepts, their aspirations are fully realized;
donning the armor of patience, they instruct those who harbor anger; and with firm diligence, they achieve accomplishment that is like a diamond.
Abiding amidst turmoil while fixing the will upon meditative concentration without attachment, their wisdom is clear and lucid;
they do not loathe or revile the impurities of birth, but employ skillful means to investigate the ultimate source of the Way wherever they may be.
They cultivate a mind of loving-kindness that is serene and gentle, and they give rise to great compassion by engaging in the conduct that benefits all sentient beings. Upon seeing...
Regarding sentient beings who have not yet attained liberation, one nurtures them to bring peace and joy to their practice;
