for those who are constantly without refuge, one protects their sense faculties, practicing protective contemplation rather than seeking ultimate nirvana, thus cultivating insight.
They uphold and follow matters that are profound and difficult to fathom, which neither śrāvakas nor pratyekabuddhas can attain;
they contemplate the treasury of fundamental meanings and do not think of worldly treatises.

They extensively accommodate all living beings, adorning their bodies with the marks and signs, adorning their speech so that words and deeds correspond, and adorning their minds by never abandoning them.
The resolve for the Way brings the joy of supernatural powers, which can be universally manifested;
the mind that sustains all abodes is like the earth, upon which all sentient beings rely and look up to;
it washes away all defilements, and its burning away of all hardships and decays is like fire; the mind is like the wind, free from affliction and heat.
He wanders with unimpeded stride, his mind like space, never harboring sorrowful thoughts.
He is attached to all dharmas and has attained *dhāraṇī*; whatever he hears, he recognizes and remembers without forgetfulness.
Endowed with perfect eloquence, he delights sentient beings and joyfully provides explanations, being established by all Buddhas.

Being able to cultivate one's own mind, one brings it to purity; conforming to the *dharmadhātu*, one thoroughly understands the four kinds of nutriment and does not conceptualize various conditioned responses. With dignified deportment and ritual propriety, one purifies one’s own person; with dignified deportment and ritual propriety, one purifies the path. To cultivate right action, one fully accomplishes every movement—whether advancing or halting—and thus practices the cultivation of emptiness.

He delights in dwelling in seclusion to transform sentient beings, yet he does not loathe or disdain social gatherings; he rejoices in meditative contemplation without distressing his mind; he is never impoverished, for he possesses all the treasures of the worthy and the sages; he performs sacrifices to subdue malevolent minds; as one who roams the wilderness, he cultivates fortitude, his mind being resolute and indestructible, practicing benevolence and compassion until reaching ultimate nirvana.

Their bodies are compliant and responsive without exhaustion; their past roots of virtue and their aspirations always follow in harmony. They repay what they have previously received through mindful conduct and noble intentions; for the sake of sentient beings, they study with diligent effort. They select and uphold the essentials to exhort and transform the ignorant; the wholesome karma they cultivate is free from the fever of afflictions, and they are fully able to discern and practice great compassion.

Universally roaming everywhere, he guides others through the three vehicles without harboring any doubt. Regarding all dharmas, he is observed by the multitude; whenever questioned, he is able to answer, and none fail to look up to him with reverence. His eloquence is unimpeded, and there is none who does not accept his words. Based on his original vows, he speaks with clarity, harmony, and gentleness. Wherever he goes, all are filled with joy. His speech is timely and never misses its proper measure. His meritorious acts of giving are such that people look up to him in admiration, like the full moon; his disposition is gentle and mild, and his words are free from coarseness or harshness.

One who attains the capacity for forbearance toward all things so that the faculties do not wither, who skillfully cultivates the mind to equally ferry beings across the cycle of coming and going like a bridge; who delivers sentient beings from the waters of the four floods like a great ship; who, like a guide, leads all who come through various practices; who constantly presides over the salvation of those of diverse teachings; and who establishes the Buddha-work for the sake of the multitudes—therefore, such a person is called a Bodhisattva.
"One who does not regress from such manifold practices and other meritorious virtues, and who is endowed with inconceivable, perfect guiding wisdom, is called a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Padmaśuddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"

Now, as I observe the Bodhisattva Wordless, whose wisdom and eloquence proclaim and expound the Way of the Buddha, it will not be long before he shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of the Most Perfect Enlightenment, and turn the vast and great Wheel of the Unsurpassed Dharma.

If there should be another person who hears what the Bodhisattva Wordless has spoken, and with faith, joy, affection, and reverence, follows it without disparaging it, then before long they too shall fully attain these dharmas of merit.
The Buddha said: “So it is!
It is exactly as you have said; there is indeed no difference.”

The Bodhisattva Wordless attained the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light; in the mere instant of forming this thought, he could expound a single phrase of the Dharma through detailed analysis for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, yet its meaning would never be exhausted.
The Bodhisattva Padmaviśuddha again addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”

Have compassion for us and this assembly; as the multitude has gathered here due to our past fundamental virtues, may you adorn them for the sake of this sutra. We pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will expound and proclaim this Wisdom-Illumination Samādhi.

If there are bodhisattvas who hear this teaching, they shall all attain the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light; and those who receive it will bring great salvation to all living beings, swiftly accomplishing the unsurpassed, true, and correct path to become the Most Perfectly Awakened One.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Padmaviśuddha:
“Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall now explain for you the Samādhi of the Radiance of Wisdom.
“Excellent! [he replied.]
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
Thus, the Bodhisattva Lotus-Purity received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"O son of noble family!
That which is called 'Wisdom-Light' (Prajñāloka) refers to the radiance of the sages; for this reason, it is named Wisdom-Light."
What is the "Noble Radiance"?

It refers to that which eliminates all obscurations, fetters, defilements, and darkness; it penetrates all hindrances and is free from turbidity and weakness—therefore, it is called the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light.

The method of understanding is non-dual; that which is observed is clear and penetrating, free from hesitation. Wisdom has no peer, and one does not look up to others for support. Having extinguished all blemishes, one immediately gives rise to responsive insight, discerning *nirvāṇa* and comprehending the single wisdom. One thoroughly understands and masters the wisdom of the three periods of time: past, future, and present.

He purifies the three fields, clearly discerns the three realms, embodies the three gates of liberation, masters the three types of penetrating wisdom, widely disseminates the Three Jewels, fully elucidates the Three Vehicles, purifies the three eyes, destroys the root of the three defilements, clarifies the three lofty assemblies, and brings certainty to those who were previously unsettled!
This is called the three steep accumulations.

Consciousness flows into the mind, intellect, and consciousness, where it discriminates the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*). It realizes the conditions of dependent origination and the correspondence of cause and effect, thereby severing lack of discipline, lack of concentration, dullness, doubt, and false views.

They understand and know the dharma-realm and can explain its primordial non-existence; they examine it as it truly is at the ultimate limit, possessing the most supreme and foremost skillful means of the Sages.

They clearly recognize all written characters and sounds; wherever they enter, whether in venerable discourse or preaching, their words are never disparaged, and their unimpeded eloquence cannot be restrained by anyone.

If one expounds the Dharma such that none can suppress it, one knows that all faculties are distinct; one decisively discerns the sources of the supple, the inferior, and the intermediate; one enters the three teachings through clarity and non-clarity; and by upholding what is appropriate, one enters into dhāraṇī.
The Samādhi of Radiant Pervasiveness Returning to the Sun’s Course, the Samādhi of Immeasurable Verses,
the Samādhi of Discerning and Proclaiming the Vajra Maṇḍala, the Vajra-like Samādhi, the Samādhi of Awakening to Angerlessness,
the Samādhi of Courageous Mind, the Samādhi of Subduing and Eliminating the Realm of Māra, the Samādhi of Solar Radiance, and the Samādhi of Illuminating Māra.
The Samādhi of Non-illumination of the Objectless Realm; the Samādhi of the Banner-Pinnacle of Entering Non-conceptualization through Boundless Wisdom;
the Samādhi of the Illuminating Flower of Pure Cultivation and Intimate Approach to All Dharmas;
the Samādhi of Entering Sound by Emitting Immeasurable Light; the Samādhi of Discerning the Virtuous Affairs and Destinations of All Sounds; and the Universal Ability to...
The Samādhi of Abiding Well in All Meritorious Deeds; the Samādhi of Radiant Light that Knows the Foundation of All Dharmas;
the Samādhi of the Sovereign King who Equally Enters the Minds of All Sentient Beings;
the Samādhi of Distinguishing All Dharmas Thoroughly and Exhaustively Without Abiding; and the Samādhi of Realizing the Equality of All and Being Free from Anger.

They possess the samādhi of the ultimate and eternal non-existence and immovability of all phenomena, the samādhi of non-attachment to the hooks and fetters of all phenomena, and the samādhi of transforming and liberating all views by transcending their manifestations; thus, they are unobstructed and unimpeded regarding all wisdom.
The Buddha said, “Son of good family!
Such categories as these comprise sixty thousand samādhis; in the past, when I saw the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and received his prediction of enlightenment, I immediately attained all these samādhis.”

Furthermore, one should reckon that these sixty thousand gates of samādhi all enter into the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light; the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light is the primary leader, and by entering into it, one attains great illumination.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"Just as the sun palace reflects in water, there are four things that appear which have never before arisen or been established.
What are these four?"
It eliminates all darkness, obscurations, and hindrances, radiating a light whose illumination extends far and wide, manifesting all forms and images.
Whatever ought to be done, it is all accomplished through the activities initiated by this sun.
The Samādhi of Wisdom-Light is likewise; if there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this concentration, that which has never before appeared will manifest, and four matters will also arise.
What are these four?

Having eliminated all the dust, afflictions, defilements, and darkness, they illuminate immeasurable, vast, and far-reaching wisdom; observing and perceiving the mental activities, appearances, and physical forms of all sentient beings, they provide instruction and establish the path of practice according to the three vehicles in which those beings train. This is called "indicating and establishing the work of the Path."
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"Suppose, for example, there were a great eight-sided wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), its wondrous radiance exquisitely pure and profound, free from all flaws and impurities. Placed atop a banner, it would illuminate forty yojanas; whatever the people desire or seek, they shall have their wishes fulfilled, each obtaining what they need without failing to receive their due. This great wish-fulfilling jewel is without stinginess or parsimony."
If there is a bodhisattva who attains and abides in this Samādhi of Wisdom-Light, their noble wisdom will be so transcendent and sublime that it is pure and brilliant like a wish-fulfilling jewel.

Having eliminated all afflictions, fetters, defilements, and manifold impurities, they abide in the concentration of the eightfold pure and subtle precepts and samādhi; through wisdom and liberation, they transcend the categories of knowledge and vision. Their truth is sincere and pristine, their skillful means are excellent, and their dhāraṇīs and eloquence are such that they discerningly practice patience, leaving nothing unexpressed. Because of this purity, none can withstand their brilliance.

Free from all defects, with supreme great compassion as his great banner, he illuminates all immeasurable Buddha-lands, so that each sentient being, according to the fundamental vows of their own mind, attains complete liberation.
"In this way, the Bodhisattva rescues those hindered within the five destinies and three realms, leading them all to the Great Way, yet remains free from conceptualization.
The Buddha told the son of good family: "It is like empty space;

empty space is boundless and can fully contain all Buddha-lands. It sustains all waters, and even when all fires burn in the kalpa-ending conflagration, it provides no place for sentient beings to advance or retreat. It allows them to find refuge and acts as their dwelling place. The domain of empty space is vast, remote, profound, and expansive—immeasurable and without obstruction."

The Samādhi of Wisdom-Light is likewise so. If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this concentration, they act as a guide to all dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings; those who have no refuge find refuge therein. Through the retribution of the causes and conditions of planting many roots of virtue, they open and understand their own minds, and for the sake of countless sentient beings, they show the path, providing instruction and the eye. For those multitudes of living beings who are stubborn regarding causes and conditions, who have not attained liberation, and who forever dwell in false views, they listen to their needs and reveal the proper place.

Suppose there were a person who, though not having established the roots of virtue and not yet returned to the vessel of the Way, nor being situated in the groundless state, is individually transformed and shown the vast vessel; who manifests the aspiration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and is shown the station of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; and who, upon hearing my preaching of the Dharma, immediately accepts and practices it, thereby attaining its fruit and retribution.

For those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who aspire to their respective vehicles, you should proclaim the essentials of the six canonical scriptures that they have previously forgotten, leading them to enter the Dharma-gate.

For this reason, for the multitude of Bodhisattvas who seek the Way, you should extensively proclaim the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), the four immeasurable minds (catvāry apramāṇāni), and the skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) to encourage and assist them in pointing out the Way. You should explain these to each of them so that their hearts may rejoice, ensuring they do not regress and attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi); this is how you reveal the locus for all classes of sentient beings.
In this regard, what is meant by "the locus for the manifestation of all dharmas"?

Suppose a bodhisattva were to personally expound the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma scriptures; if there are sentient beings who come with doubts and indecision to seek instruction, the bodhisattva always maintains a resolute mind and single-mindedly resolves each person's entanglements and obstructions.

The meaning of a single phrase, though expounded and analyzed throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, is immeasurable, profound, vast, and far-reaching; it is unimpeded and inexhaustible, without limit or boundary—this is that which reveals the locus of all dharmas.
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"It is like the light of a great torch that shines afar; all things that are covered, obscured, or hidden—whether forms or colors—are made manifest by it!"
Such is the benefit brought by the radiance of a torch.

The clarity of wisdom and the concentration of the mind are likewise so: if there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this concentration, they can, with a single mind of luminous wisdom, manifest the chapters and verses so that all the immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as well as all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and sentient beings, behold them; yet they do not deviate from their resolve nor shift from their state of mind, for the scope of the mind of luminous wisdom is boundless.
The Buddha told the son of good family:

"The abode of wisdom and clarity dwells within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), perceiving the source of all dharmas; within the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), it gives rise to the source of wisdom for those who have not yet generated the intent; within the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), it is the source of tranquility for body and mind; and within the faculties (*indriya*), it is the source of noble penetration."
What is meant by "powers"? It refers to the power of wisdom, which enters the source of insight through the factors of enlightenment and the bases of mental engagement.

What is meant by the "Path"? It abides in the source of right view; the one who observes in stillness contemplates tranquility; the one who practices with sincerity is at the source of skillful cessation. The Noble Truths are the source of skillful, quiescent wisdom; that to which mindfulness returns is the source of the true meaning of the goal; the one who discerns the Path is at the source of the Dharma and its meaning; the one who attains supernormal powers is at the source of the exhaustion of outflows. The practice of the holy life arises from the source of great compassion and the four immeasurable minds; it is the source of universal mindfulness and reflection upon the Dharma. Among all the perfections (*pāramitās*), the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is the primary source.
Skillful means respond to the source of sentient beings' minds; as for the ten powers, they consist in knowing the finite and the infinite, and the possible and the impossible—this is their source.
As for the fearlessnesses, they consist in clearly comprehending the source of the equal Buddha-way.
Regarding the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): they are unhindered in their source throughout the three periods of time.

What is called "the eye" refers to the Buddha’s eye, which adorns his body; its source cannot be seen even by the mark between the eyebrows at the crown of his head. What adorns his mouth refers to the proclamation of the sūtras and the Dharma, whose source is free from any impairment. What adorns his mind refers to the practice of samādhi and meditative concentration, whose source is unwavering.
O son of good family!
All dharmas ultimately converge upon the source of wisdom; this is what is called the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light, the fountainhead and foremost source of all dharmas.
When these words were spoken, the Bodhisattva Padmavyūha attained this Wisdom-Light Samādhi, and ten thousand other bodhisattvas likewise attained this samādhi;
the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and a great radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions.
At that time, all those gathered in the assembly—the devas and the people—each brought flowers as offerings and scattered them over the Buddha.
Then, the multitude of bodhisattvas in the assembly who were resolved upon the Mahāyāna addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We have never before heard the name of this samādhi, much less its extensive explanation and analytical meaning."

"By the merit of the offerings we have now made to the World-Honored One, may we attain this samādhi and progress therein step by step; through this vow, may we certainly attain this state of meditative concentration without doubt."

It is for our great benefit and to bring us auspicious joy that we have encountered and heard this samādhi. If anyone hears of this samādhi and rejoices with faith, their merit and blessings will be beyond measure; they shall never deviate from the bodhicitta, and before long they too shall attain this samādhi.
The Buddha said: "So it is! It is just as you have said, without any difference."
Those who lack virtue do not plant the roots of goodness and thus cannot encounter this samādhi;
how much less could there be anyone who, upon hearing it, would respond with joy and faith? Such a thing has never occurred.
"Only if one is in the presence of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or follows an enlightened teacher can one truly believe in and delight in this meditative concentration.

Just as the Buddha had finished speaking these words, a bodhisattva emerged from the navel of the World-Honored One. His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, colored like purple-gold, and his appearance was embellished by the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
As soon as it emerged from the navel, the body of that Bodhisattva immediately radiated a towering, infinite, and magnificent brilliance, completely eclipsing all other lights;
only the light of the World-Honored One remained uniquely manifest.
Then that bodhisattva prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and standing before him, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jñānaprabhāsa respectfully inquires after you: Are you well and at ease? Is your movement vigorous? Is your gait light and agile? Is your strength and vigor secure?”
I have sent forth inquiries to the Great Sage regarding these sixty *koṭi-nayuta* bodhisattvas who have come to this assembly to hear the sūtras.

They pay homage to the World-Honored One, prostrating themselves to receive his instruction; furthermore, they wish to see the bodhisattvas from the great assemblies of the worlds of the ten directions and the Bodhisattva Without Speech, and to hear the wisdom and eloquence with which they expound the Dharma, so as to receive teachings never heard before and to listen to this samādhi of Wisdom-Light.

O God among Gods, please preach the Dharma to the bodhisattvas according to their needs, so that they may attain this Wisdom-Illumination Samādhi, achieve the infinite radiance of the Great Dharma, and frequently travel to this buddha-field.
Thereupon, Śāriputra stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Where does the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jñānaprabhāsa reside?"
Are you currently preaching the Dharma in this present world?
How far is it from here, and what is the nature of that land?
Furthermore, please tell us the name of this noble being, as well as where those sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas reside.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"To the east of here, past as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a world named Dwelling on the Firm Root of Vajra. The Tathāgata Wisdom-Grasping Radiance resides in that land; he is currently present there."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Why is that world named 'Abiding in the Root of Firm Vajra'?
From the bottom to the top of its lower ground, it is extremely firm and solid, indestructible, and entirely composed of vajra."
All of this is brought about by the power of that Buddha’s original vows. Why is this so?

Because that Buddha’s adamantine practice of firm resolve is peerless and without difficulty; and because the various bodhisattvas who have undertaken adamantine practices are courageous and steadfast, such that none can destroy them. It is through the majesty and perfect endowment of his own sovereign power that it is thus!

If the world were composed of clay, it would surely break apart, crumble, and scatter into minute fragments; yet if there were someone born in that world, their body—being like a diamond—would likewise be so firm as to be indestructible.
For this reason, that land is named "Abiding in the Root of Firm Vajra.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, as to what you have asked regarding the name of this bodhisattva: [he is named]... (the name follows).
He is named Vajranābhi.

This Bodhisattva Vajranābhi, in the mere space of a single thought-moment, passes through the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains and transcends Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; he emerges from the navels of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all of which are established by the majestic spiritual power and merit of those Buddhas, as well as by his own wisdom of the six supernormal knowledges and the power of his psychic faculties. For this reason, the Bodhisattva is named Vajranābhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
As for your previous question regarding where the assembly of sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas resides,
you should ask this of the True Man (bhadravarga), and he will provide you with an answer.
The worthy Śāriputra asked the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha:
"O son of noble family!
Where do these sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas abide?"
Vajragarbha replied:
“The Buddha has praised you, Venerable Śāriputra, as having the most honored wisdom.
With the eye of wisdom, O Worthy One, investigate from beginning to end: where do these bodhisattvas reside?”
At that time, Śāriputra, with his noble eye of wisdom, searched everywhere for the bodhisattvas but did not know where they were.
The Bodhisattva Vajranābhi replied,
“Venerable Śāriputra!
"Let us seek out those of our own kind who study with us and share our resolve for liberation.
Then Śāriputra said to Aniruddha, "The Buddha has praised you, Venerable One, as having the most supreme divine eye; let us seek out where he is."

Then Aniruddha, with his pure celestial eye that transcends those of gods and humans, searched throughout the trichiliocosm; he looked upon it as if observing a fruit or a precious jewel in the palm of his hand, yet he could never find any of the bodhisattvas, nor did he see where they resided.
The worthy Aniruddha replied to Śāriputra:
"I have searched everywhere, yet I can never know where these bodhisattvas reside.
The Vajranābhi Bodhisattva said to Śāriputra:
“Virtuous ones, you possess only the fleshly eye; it cannot be said that you possess the divine eye.
How is it that while contemplating together with samādhi and dhyāna, you survey all the lands yet do not see those lands, nor do you see where the assembly of bodhisattvas dwells?”
Śāriputra asked:
"Virtuous son of noble family!
What is the nature of the divine eye?"
"Is it that we and those like us have never seen such a thing?
Vajragarbha replied, "Indeed, Śāriputra!"
My divine eye has never seen form.
Śāriputra and the other great disciples among my followers have been unable to see me since the beginning; what kind of quality does this divine eye possess?
"Furthermore, there is none who can withstand his towering brilliance.
Śāriputra again asked the son of good family:
"What kind of forms and images did you see?"
Yet you say that we have never seen them before.
Vajranābhi replied, “Elder,
have you ever seen those who dwell in the world-system of Solid Vajra, or the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jñānāvabhāsa?”
Śāriputra replied, "Today we have heard the name of that world; by what cause can it be seen?
Vajragarbha said:

"O Śāriputra! Such categories as these—inconceivable and incalculable Buddha-lands, along with their various bodhisattvas, retinues, and sentient beings—each have different destinies and distinct modes of birth."

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives all of these with his divine eye; there is nothing left out or not encompassed by it. Although all Pratyekabuddhas possess the divine eye, they cannot behold them—how much less could Śrāvakas possibly see them?

When these words were spoken, sixty thousand people who had previously sought the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were filled with great joy; they immediately resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and simultaneously raised their voices in a cry of praise, saying:
"May we ourselves obtain the Buddha’s Dharma-eye; we have no further need for the divine eyes of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas!"
"Shadows, coverings, and obstructions—
none of these can limit or hinder the Buddha’s Dharma-eye. Thereupon,
the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, according to his true form, entered right concentration (*samādhi*) to establish a responsive manifestation and displayed his supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*).

The sacred intent of the Buddha, the transformative majesty of the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, and the immeasurable power of their lofty roots of merit from past lives caused all those gathered in the assembly to behold with their own eyes sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas, each seated cross-legged upon lotus flowers at various points upon the Buddha’s body, with palms joined as they listened to the sutra. They were neither too close to the Buddha’s body nor too far away; this was entirely due to the infinite resonance of the Tathāgata’s vast grace.
Furthermore, the body of the World-Honored One neither increased nor decreased, remaining entirely unobstructed; it appeared exactly as before, without any diminution.

The entire assembly was filled with wonder and joy, leaping for gladness at such an unprecedented occurrence. With single-minded devotion, they joined their palms in homage and stood before the Buddha, each exclaiming in praise:
"How inconceivable!"
How difficult it is to fathom!

The physical forms of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are vast and long, their majestic holiness immeasurable, and their miraculous transformations and meritorious virtues beyond all calculation. Yet they are able to accommodate sixty billion *ya* of beings, who sit within the Buddha’s body to listen to the sutras, while the original sacred body of the Buddha is seen to neither increase nor decrease.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha surveyed the entire assembly and raised his voice, declaring:
"For this reason, you should all understand it together!

The body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the Dharma-body; it is vast and infinite. There is no mark or sign that is not perfectly proportioned, and the body has no boundaries, being immeasurable."

In the mere instant that the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, directs his intention, he causes all the waters existing within the trichiliocosm—the great oceans, rivers, streams, springs, and sources—as well as the lands, provinces, groves, grasses, trees, mountains, and earth, to enter entirely into the Buddha’s body without increasing or decreasing, yet they all appear exactly as they were before.

Furthermore, O worthy ones, there are countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas from various Buddha-lands, numbering in the tens of millions, who behold from afar the World-Honored One’s subtle and wondrous radiance and his pure, stainless marks and signs; they all set out to come and see the Holy Honored One to inquire after and receive the scriptures.
For the sake of all under heaven, he exhorted the devas, humans, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings to provide protection and refuge, so that they might go to listen to the sutra.
If they were not to come, they would not perceive the transformation of the Way and would be unable to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.

Because the Buddha desires to open, transform, and deliver sentient beings, the Tathāgata takes these bodhisattvas and places them within his own body, so that they may hear and receive the Dharma without encountering obstacles or experiencing any doubt or difficulty.

There may be bodhisattvas who, dwelling within the earth, enter into jeweled lattices and perceive themselves seated upon lotus flowers; all this is moved by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, whose virtue and wisdom are sublime, lofty, and immeasurable.

Then, receiving the Buddha’s holy command and the power of the adamantine navel and his supreme vows, sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas all emerged simultaneously from the pores of the Great Sage. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and each, by the power of their majestic virtue and supernormal faculties, manifested a subtle and exquisite throne and sat upon it.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
For what reason is the Bodhisattva Acalavāk named ‘Silent’?”
The Buddha said,
"You yourself should ask this of the True Man (sajjana),
and he shall explain it for you. Then Vajranābhi asked Avākya:
“O virtuous son of noble family!
For what reason do you call yourself ‘The Wordless’?
The Wordless remained silent.
When he had asked this three times and still received no reply,
Vajranābhi questioned him again, saying:
"For what reason do you not answer me after being asked three times?"
The Silent One replied:
"I have sought the source of these words and never found it; for this reason, I do not answer you!
Furthermore, son of good family!"
In principle, it is not appropriate to question one who is without words; for what reason, then, do you address him as "Wordless"?
To calculate his state of being wordless, there are neither verbal expressions nor vocal sounds.
Vajranābhi asked again:
"If there is no speech, for what reason do you now speak with your mouth? Wu-yen replied:
"I have fully emulated everything spoken by all the Buddhas, and I have likewise emulated everything spoken by sentient beings.
He asked again:
"In what way did you emulate what was spoken by all the Buddhas?"
He replied:
“Just as all Buddhas have expounded the Dharma of the sutras, I receive their majestic spiritual power through the strength of my own mind; it is likewise so.

For this reason, I now follow entirely what all Buddhas have spoken, employing their vocal tones and equalizing the written characters. Without any distortion, I expound the Dharma of the sutras; this is what it means to model oneself after what all Buddhas have spoken.”
He asked again:
"In what way, then, do you imitate the speech of sentient beings?
He replied:
"According to the sounds, voices, and languages of all classes of people and sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma for them.
This is to emulate what all sentient beings and people say."
He asked again:
“Noble son! How much time has passed since you lost your speech?”
He replied,
"Since the time I lost mindfulness.
He asked again:
“Noble son! What does this statement mean?
He replied:
"For this reason, he does not engage in mental recollection, yet it is not that he does not find joy; his mind has no objects of thought, and thus his mouth remains silent.
He asked again: "Noble son!"
From where do words emerge?
Do they emerge from the mind,
or do they emerge from the body?
He replied:
"It does not issue from the body, nor does it issue from the mind. Why is this so?"
"The body does not exist eternally and lacks autonomy; its mind is like an illusion.
For this reason, [the Dharma] does not emerge from the body, nor does it emerge from the mind.
He asked again:
“From where does it emerge?
He replied,
“If you wish to ask this, from where do the words and phrases you speak themselves emerge?”
Does it emerge from emptiness?
Emptiness has no form and is invisible.
Now you ask me this; by what means is it so?
He said, "It truly depends on emptiness, being without view and without form.
He replied:

"Therefore, son of good family, that which is spoken is like space and cannot be seen; what you have asked is likewise according to those words, and is also like space and cannot be seen. Space is thus forever invisible and possesses no marks."
For this reason, when one seeks all dharmas and their verbal expressions, they are entirely unobtainable.

Just as verbal expressions are unobtainable when sought, all dharmas are tranquil and serene; the discourse of words and phrases is likewise so, for all dharmas are like human speech, suddenly unknown as to where they abide.

Speech is like space, having no place where it can be seen; all phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise like space and have no location. That which is called speech is a composite of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); all phenomena likewise arise from conditions. If one seeks the source and locus of all phenomena, one cannot find where those conditions themselves arise.
That which cannot be apprehended does not arise, and thus it is not born.
Furthermore, that which does not arise does not emerge; that which does not emerge does not manifest.

That which is without origination has no trace of the eye, nor any trace of forms; it has no trace of consciousness, nor any trace of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; it has no trace of phenomena, nor any trace of mental consciousness.
That which leaves no trace has neither going nor coming; that which has neither going nor coming is called "walking alone.
One who walks alone has nowhere to go and perceives nothing within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). You should contemplate in this way: can one truly behold that which was originally unseen?
He asked again:
"Why did you not see it before?
He replied:
“Neither arising nor originating.
He asked again,
“In what sense are they neither arising nor originating?”
He replied,
"That which cannot be examined has no coming.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'that which cannot be observed has no coming'?
He replied:
"Space is invisible; it has no coming."
Space is equal, and all dharmas are likewise equal to space.
For this reason, the equality of all dharmas is also like space; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are without partiality and are equal to space.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'all dharmas are equal to space'?
He replied:
Because there is no counterpart and because all Buddhas are equal, all dharmas are ultimately equal.
They were originally equal in the past, they are equal in the future, and they are equal in the present; there is no differentiation.
Considering all these things, by means of the primordial limit (*koṭi*) of all dharmas, they are thus and according to reality; the primordial limit has no origin.
The primordial limit is according to reality; the primordial limit is according to scrutiny.
The ultimate limit has no origin; the ultimate limit is equal and without distinction. This is what is called the absence of two limits and the absence of multiplicity.
What is meant by "two"?
To reckon in terms of "self" and "mine" is called duality; if one does not crave the body and does not reckon in terms of "self" and "mine," then there is no duality.
What is meant by duality?

When there is the eye and visible forms, it is called duality; the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—these are called duality.
To state the essential point: if one harbors attachment to any phenomena, this is called "duality.
Even that which gives rise to duality cannot be apprehended. Why is this so?

When one contemplates that there is nothing to be attained, then there is no duality, nor are there words; as for this Dharma, the mind, the mental faculty, and all consciousness—if one does not cultivate these three things, it is called non-duality.
This non-duality should not be expounded. Why is this?
That which is spoken of does not transcend duality; that which is unspeakable is precisely the absence of duality.
He asked again:
"Regarding what you call 'non-duality,' who is it that creates duality?
He replied:
"That which is non-dual cannot be made dual. Why is this?
Even if one were to employ various skillful means to attempt to transform the non-dual so that it becomes dual, it could never be established."
He asked again:
"Are the laws and teachings you have spoken dualistic,
or are they non-dual?"
He replied:
"That which constitutes the Dharma and Vinaya is non-dual;
it is firm and difficult to shift."

Why is this? Because there is no verbal sign of confusion, nor is there anything to be governed; by means of non-verbal discourse one guides them, such that nothing can destroy it, it cannot be impaired or deficient, and because it is indestructible, it is called "firm guidance," which is without duality.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi addressed the Buddha, saying: “So be it,
World-Honored One!”
"Whatever the Bodhisattva Wordless (*Avāca*) proclaims is entirely due to the heroic grace of the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light (*Prajñā-āloka*).
The Buddha said, "It is as you have said;
all is indeed the majestic grace of the Samādhi of Wisdom-Light!"
At that time, the bodhisattvas who had come from the land of Grasping Wisdom Radiance asked the Silent One:
"Virtuous son of good family!
What dharma have you studied such that your eloquence and wisdom are so towering and immeasurable?"
Wuyou replied,
"As the Buddha has taught, all dharmas are established through precepts.
He asked again:
“O son of good family!
Would you deign to look upon us with compassion and, for our sake, analyze, expound, and establish the precepts?
He replied:
“Wise one! That which does not abide in body, nor abide in speech or mind, this is the establishment of the precept.
That which does not abide in the internal, nor the external, nor in between, this is the establishment of the precept.”
If there is no thought and no reflection, nor any matter of instruction or speech, this is called establishing the precept.
To have neither response nor non-response, neither mindfulness nor non-mindfulness, and likewise no divergent thoughts—this is called establishing the precept.

Not abiding in the wholesome nor in the unwholesome, not dwelling in the world nor transcending the world; neither existing nor non-existing, neither harming nor non-harming, neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, neither unconditioned nor conditioned, neither birth-and-death nor extinction—this is called establishing the precepts.
Even if one were to establish such a comparison and abide in the precepts, one would not abide in any phenomena; not dwelling upon any phenomena, one would not form the thought:
"I have something to say, to proclaim, or to analyze."
Therefore, worthy one!
This is called admonition.
Whatever is spoken abides in duality; yet its true ultimate limit, as well as its place of abiding, reaches back to the rootless.

Furthermore, regarding the sphere of the Dharma-realm, it is by abiding therein that I discourse; yet that which is discoursed upon can never be apprehended. That which is spoken is likewise without recollection, and that which is proclaimed is without conceptualization.
He asked again:
"Son of good family!
Regarding that which is unobtainable, free from mental recollection, and devoid of conceptualization—what speech can there be concerning it?"
He replied:
"It is the natural order that cannot be grasped; it is without recollection and without conceptual thought—it is spoken of as being spontaneous!
He asked again:
"Who was it that spoke to him regarding what he declined?
He replied,
"O Worthy One!"
That which I have renounced is extinguished at that very moment and does not arise again. Why is this?
All the dharmas taught previously ultimately return to extinction; all dharmas are entirely without arising.

The dharmas that arise cannot be known as having a location; though they manifest forms in the present, they are entirely devoid of form and have no place from which they can be apprehended. Why is this?
Because these are empty and exhausted, lacking all marks; their fundamental limit (pūrvakoṭi) is beyond verbal teaching.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said:
"One cannot conceive of or grasp a past mind; it is the same for the future and the present!
Arising and ceasing in an instant, shattered and utterly consumed, it is violent and easily transformed; its form and likeness are impossible to seize."

Their desires, grasping, attachments, and conceptualizations are false; their reliance on feelings and thoughts is entirely like a magical illusion. Therefore, when one investigates all that is spoken to its ultimate limit, it is entirely empty and without reality; its meaning cannot be attained, nor can it be explained, nor can it be proclaimed by mouth or conceived by mind!

Why is this so? Because there is nothing created and no practice; for one who understands and awakens to this meaning, they no longer employ verbal expressions, nor do they have any thoughts with the mind!

Whatever is proclaimed and explained through analytical discourse is like the sound of an echo responding to a call; it is like the proclamations made by a manifested Tathāgata, and what that person teaches is likewise such.
This is the meaning guaranteed by all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and all people of the world; it is inconceivable!
Their skillful means cannot be obstructed, and the Dharma established through their eloquent discourse cannot be moved or shifted.
At that time, the bodhisattvas praised the Silent One, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Son of good family!"
"Please speak these words.

We too have heard this entry into the Dharma-gate; that which is returned to as a gate is truly no gate at all, being equal to empty space. The Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the various Bodhisattvas have now spoken thus, and what we have received is likewise so."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi asked the Bodhisattva Avākya:
"Come, son of good family!
Let us go together to the world-system called Firmly Established Vajra-Root, to see the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jñānadhvaja, and to behold that land."
Wuyuan replied:

"Furthermore, noble son, this is where I have heard that the World-Honored One Wisdom-Light, who dwells in the world of Firm Vajra Roots, is also present here; why then should I abandon this place to go elsewhere?"
Vajragarbha asked:
"This world is composed of earth and mud; it is not made of vajra.
Vimalakīrti replied with silence.

“Son of good family, at the very moment you conceive this thought, you shall transcend Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, passing through the Iron Ring Mountains without obstruction. Are you able to take up a single particle of dust from this Buddha-land? If not, then you should know that this world is composed of clay.”

Upon hearing these words, Bodhisattva Aśabdha immediately entered the samādhi of the Vajra-maṇḍala; at that very moment, this trichiliocosm was spontaneously transformed into something exceedingly vast, firm, and indestructible, entirely composed of vajra.

Thereupon, Vajragarbha manifested great power and displayed miraculous transformations; donning the armor of firm and virtuous precepts, he attempted to lift a single grain of dust from this earth but was unable to do so. He thought to himself:
"How extraordinary and unprecedented! Is this the sublime manifestation established by this Great Sage?"
"Is this what has been inspired and aroused by the Unspoken?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed it is!"
World-Honored One!

At the very moment I first resolved my mind [for enlightenment] in the past, I passed through the Iron Ring Mountains and the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and traversed as many Buddha-lands as there are sands in the Ganges River.
"Now I wish to lift a single grain of dust from this land, yet I am unable to do so.
O God among Gods!
By whose majestic power and spiritual authority has this been established?"
"Is this the compassionate and holy intent of the God among Gods?
Or is it a transformation brought about by the Wordless?
The Buddha said:
"This is established by the Bodhisattva Avāca! Why is this so?

Because the Bodhisattva Avāca, through his absorption in the Vajra-maṇḍala-samādhi, has caused this great trichiliocosm to become exceedingly firm and solid, indestructible, and entirely composed of vajra."

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this samādhi, they may exercise their will at pleasure; whatever number of buddha-fields they wish to transform so that they all become adamantine, it shall immediately be as they intend.

The noble mind of wisdom arises and manifests the Way and its Virtue; by means of this samādhi and through right reception, it causes all buddha-fields to become entirely adamantine, incapable of being destroyed or touched—this is the majestic and numinous realm of this samādhi.
Thereupon, Vajragarbha and his retinue of sixty quadrillion bodhisattvas came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By practicing what dharma can a bodhisattva attain the Vajra-maṇḍala Samādhi?"
The Buddha told the son of good family:
“A bodhisattva possesses four dharmas by which they attain this Vajra-Dharmadhātu Samādhi. What are these four?
The first is to maintain one's resolve as firm as a vajra, constantly cherishing the mind of the Way to transcend all roots of merit.
The second is to be fully endowed with virtuous conduct, cultivating and refining skillful means throughout incalculable kalpas to adorn the great enterprise.
The third is to enter into the profound Dharma and discern the source of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The fourth is to possess complete noble wisdom without any deficiency or omission.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four things by which one finds self-delight. What are these four?
First, transcending [the world] with wisdom and being fully endowed with the five supernormal powers.

The second is the gate of liberation consisting of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, wherein one enters samādhi with right reception, and the mind does not wander or dissipate, but finds its own delight therein.
The third is establishing oneself in the precepts and abiding in the dharma-realm, dwelling in a sourceless state to achieve the clarity of wisdom.
The fourth is the meaning of ultimate sincerity and profound depth: clearly understanding the meaning of the sutras and attaining mastery over all dharmas of quiescence.
Furthermore, there are four [other qualities]. What are these four?
First, to abide in great compassion and cultivate the four Brahma-vihāras;
second, to practice the Prajñāpāramitā and the six pāramitās;
third, to employ skillful means (upāya-kauśalya) and practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
The fourth is to cultivate the doors of liberation and the four noble truths for the sake of all sentient beings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four.
What are the four?
First, the karma created by the body is like a vajra.
Second, that which is spoken by the mouth is pure, subtle, and gentle, also like a vajra.
The third is that his mind is held with such firm resolve that it cannot be shaken or moved, being like a vajra.
The fourth is that his will and nature are steadfast and courageous, such that they cannot be destroyed.
These are the four dharmas.
"The practices of the bodhisattvas will swiftly lead them to attain this Vajra-Dharmodgata Samādhi.
When these words were spoken, those bodhisattvas immediately attained this Vajra-Dharmodgata Samādhi.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Wordless addressed his father, General Siṃha:

"Great Man, have you not seen how the Buddhas appear in the world? Their reputation for virtuous fragrance and their majestic holiness are immeasurable; their wisdom of the Way is lofty and far-reaching, transcending all and peerless—this is something never before encountered."
Inconceivable!
Inconceivable!
Such a likeness is beyond all analogy; that which was originally cherished with sorrow is now fully manifested!
For the sake of immeasurable classes of sentient beings, you have guided and shown them the way to extinction and the ultimate great peace.
We only pray that the Great Being will give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
General Siṃha replied to Aniruddha:
"You should know this: seven days after my birth, a celestial being came to command me and informed me to resolve upon the Great Way."

The Buddha is the God among Gods; through the vision of his Way, he knows my resolve and character. My mind, day and night, contemplates the Buddha-way, and I have no other teacher toward whom I could turn my heart for refuge; I shall take refuge only in the Infinite Great Sage.

General Siṃha, the First Lady, their sons and daughters, and five hundred kinsmen and attendants from both inside and outside the family all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Wordless replied to his parents, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, and the great assembly:
"O virtuous ones, today you have conceived the Great Resolve; you should now practice with diligent vigor to adorn the mind of the Way."
He immediately asked:
"What is meant by 'adorning the mind with the resolve for the path'?
Wuyanyan replied:
“There are forty matters that adorn the mind set on the Way. What are these forty?
First, possessing ultimate faith in the Buddha’s Way so that the mind does not doubt or disparage it; second, rejoicing in the Dharma and causing it to endure for a long time.”
1. To be free from pride toward the noble assembly and to be respectful and humble; 2. To always cultivate association with virtuous friends; 3.

To regard all bodhisattvas as one would the Buddha upon seeing them; 4. Never to harbor malice toward sentient beings; 5. To reverently serve and attend upon elders and those who are sources of blessings;
6. To maintain a mind of equanimity toward both the beloved and the hateful; 7. To enter into the Dharma without weariness; 8. To be diligent.
10. Listening to the sūtras; 1. Hearing and inclining toward the noble training; 2. Explaining them for the sake of others;
3. Having a mind free from expectation; 4. The Dharma being without a teacher; 5. Mindfulness according to what is appropriate;
6. Practicing without a basis; 7. Not cherishing anything that is beloved; 8. Following the prohibitions and precepts without ever failing or leaking.
1. Proclaiming and disseminating the power of patience; 2. Practicing diligence so that it is all-encompassing; 3.
Causing the thorough cultivation of meditative concentration and single-mindedness, while remaining in accord with the category of wisdom;
4. Using skillful means to transform and enlighten sentient beings; 5. Never forgetting or abandoning those whom one has exhorted and assisted.
1. Protecting the masses according to their needs; 2. Self-disciplining one’s own mind while subduing the intentions of others; 3. Originally lacking not even a single dharma; 4.

Not becoming attached to worldly defilements when providing instruction on desires; 5. Constantly abandoning clamor and bustle, delighting in tranquility; 6. Regarding dwelling in seclusion as a mark of virtue; 7. Cultivating the conduct of sages while knowing the limits of moderation; 8. Always practicing contentment that cannot be shaken; 9. Remaining amidst worldly laws without being defiled by them; 10. Yet remaining compliant with the six firm dharmas; 11. Furthermore, not abandoning or neglecting the practice of the four debts of gratitude; 12. Constantly honoring and following firm vows and aspirations; 13. Never destroying or losing the root of virtuous merit; 14. Being without negligence regarding the studies one has undertaken; 15. Taking no pleasure in the Lesser Vehicle; 16. The bodhicitta being unshakable—these are the forty [qualities].

With profound faith in the subtle and wondrous, their resolve is neither timid nor weak; they abandon all evil without transgression or failure, fully possessing every merit and virtue, and gathering together a treasury of immeasurable blessings and renown. Cherishing and wearing the Dharma within their hearts, they abide in the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) without ever regressing.
These are the forty practices of a great man that manifest all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms!

Adorning oneself with the precious mind of the Way through these merits, at the very moment one resolves the mind, the roots of virtue arising within the realm of the trichiliocosm Buddhas will all appear before one’s eyes, no longer needing to be sought afar.
"It is like the sun’s chariot dwelling in the void, shining everywhere without exception.
General Siṃha replied to his son:

"Virtuous one, you should come and go frequently so that we may remember each other and meet; through this, I shall instruct and admonish you, providing support and protection so that you do not regress from the ultimate, unsurpassed, true, and right path."
Wu Yan replied:
"Great Being, if you wish to know, there are furthermore ten dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas, which all Buddhas and Great Beings constantly keep in mind."
What are these ten? They are:
constantly practicing diligence with the desire to bring peace to sentient beings, without thinking of attaining great peace for oneself alone;
possessing physical strength and vigor to encourage and inspire many; and seeing those who are weak and frail, one comforts and consoles them.
All roots of virtue they have cultivated, they relinquish by giving them to all people, never harboring any anxiety.
Those whom they transform and inspire toward the Way don the great armor of virtue and make this vow:
"If these sentient beings attain the Buddha-way and receive the True Dharma, I shall provide for them with offerings and serve them."
"Only then shall I attain supreme perfect enlightenment.

For the sake of the True Dharma, he sacrifices his body and life; he does not abandon the orthodox scriptures, but proclaims and analyzes the meaning of even a single chapter, circulating it throughout all beings for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Donning the great armor of virtue, they do not grow weary nor harbor cowardice.
All dharmas are fundamentally pure;

even upon hearing these words, they do not feel fear. They do not restrict themselves to the Great Way, nor do they abandon the Buddha-dharma, nor do they regard it as empty. That which they observe and perceive, they know to be truly non-illusory.

Being equal to the self, one is also equal to all sentient beings; being equal to sentient beings, one is equal to the Dharma. By being equal to the sutras and the Dharma, one then gains faith and delight in the equality of empty space; one does not fall into the extremes of śamatha and vipaśyanā, nor does one again fall into the path of birth, old age, sickness, death, affliction, and calamity.

They are seen by all the world as wavering and shifting; they labor diligently amidst the defilements of countless multitudes, and whatever is incited by the various Māras and Pāpīyans, they speak of these many difficulties to issue warnings and slanders, saying:
"The Buddha-way is difficult to attain and the sutra-dharma is difficult to encounter; it would be better to seek the state of a Śrāvaka early on so as to cross over swiftly!"

Upon hearing this, the Bodhisattva firmly maintains a single mind and resolves upon the infinite vow, never becoming weary or disheartened; he does not retreat or turn back, nor does he abandon the Mahāyāna. He abides in the truly correct and authentic Dharma, ensuring his words correspond with his deeds and that he is never false. His bodily conduct is sincere, and he does not deceive himself before the devas, sentient beings, and the Buddhas of the ten directions—this constitutes the matter of the ten dharmas of a Great Being.
"The conduct of a bodhisattva is constantly observed and remembered by all Buddhas and all righteous beings.
When these words were spoken, General Siṃha and his retinue immediately attained the patient acceptance of accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī kṣānti).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Receive this sutra-dharma; uphold, recite, read, and fully and extensively expound it for others."
Why is this? All the Buddhas, Great Sages, and those who have arisen through the Way and its Virtue in the past, future, and present, all emerge from this gateway of the Dharma-piṭaka.

The Bodhisattva Wordless has now come here; contemplating the True Truth, he proclaims these immeasurable Dharma-gates, exhorting and transforming countless people so that they may study the Buddha-way!
Therefore, Ānanda!

Those who wish to receive and uphold the treasury of the Dharma from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, should reverently uphold this sutra and cherish it in their hearts, extensively expounding this gateway to the treasury of the Dharma for others, and inspiring countless sentient beings and people so that they may attain the path of Buddhahood.

Whether the Tathāgata is in the world or has entered parinirvāṇa, if there should be anyone who receives this sutra, it is entirely due to the establishment of the Buddha’s intent; they shall uphold, recite, read, and practice according to the instructions above.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“There are three matters for which the merit is immeasurable.
What are these three?”

First is to protect and uphold the True Dharma; second is for one’s own body to realize the mind of enlightenment; third is to exhort those who have not yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment to do so.
These are the three.
The merit and blessings of these deeds are immeasurable; even if a Tathāgata were to praise such achievements, he could never reach the end of them, let alone a śrāvaka.

At that time, there were seventy quadrillion bodhisattvas in the assembly who, upon hearing what the Buddha had said, all rose from their seats. Desiring to protect the True Dharma, they each spoke, saying:

"We, of our own kind, shall together uphold the World-Honored One’s orthodox canon and cause it to spread far and wide; we shall take up these sutra scrolls and explain them for others, exhorting them to resolve upon the path."
The Bodhisattva Wordless addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Indeed,
World-Honored One!”
“Regarding that which can be understood and clarified— the establishment of perfect enlightenment— can those dharmas be received,
grasped, or maintained? The Buddha said, “No!”
He again asked the Buddha:
"For what reason did the Buddha just now say this, that all these sons of noble family have arisen and stood up, desiring to protect the true Dharma?"
The Buddha said:

"It is because I wish to nurture the sons of noble families that I employ these forms to provide protection. I proclaim the unconditioned reality—the dharma that cannot be grasped—and through the instruction of words and letters, I protect the Dharma and comply with their intentions."
What is called "protection" means that one does not rely on verbal inquiry nor employ written words to practice the Way; this is what is termed "protecting the True Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family!
There are two matters for protecting the True Dharma. What are these two?

The first is that what is "unattainable" is precisely the attainment of the True Dharma; one should protect it by always following its course, rather than protecting it merely through verbal exposition.
The second is: not to support various falsehoods, but to be able to practice what one hears taught, without seeking fame through arrogance or indulgence.
This is the second.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, desiring to make offerings to the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Silent Speech (Avakāśa), and this sutra, rained down celestial flowers from all sides, scattering them over the Buddha and the various bodhisattvas throughout the entire great assembly. With their mouths they proclaimed these words:
"We pray that the World-Honored One Śākyamuni may long remain in the world, and that this Dharma of the sutra may spread spontaneously throughout Jambudvīpa."
The Buddha said, “So it is!

Upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, the Bodhisattva Silent Speech, General Lion, along with his retinue; the Bodhisattva Vajranābhi and the sixty billion nayutas of bodhisattvas; Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ānanda; and all the devas, worldlings, and asuras were without exception filled with joy.
